summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31.1965 and March 31st, 1967 respectively) in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,23,790/ representing interest on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed "Commissioner of Wealth tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth Tax officer appealed to the Appellate Tribunal and contended that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the respondent. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the appellant, but held that accrued Interest was liable not to be added in the Wealth tax assessments. In reference, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The concept of "net wealth" is a well recognised principle of interpretation and it cannot be disputed that the concept of net wealth is not static or static. It has been repeatedly held that the expression "net Wealth" in section 2(q) of the Wealth Act means the last day of the previous year as defined under the Income Tax Act, if an assessment were to be made under that Act for that year; and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. [310C D] 1.2 The method of accounting adopted by the assessee is not a static or rigid formula but has been evolved in many cases to determine the value of assets of an assessee. It is a matter of common knowledge that the business of the assesses is not merely a collection of money but also a realisation of money which is ultimately earned by the business. The concept, therefore, is different from the concept that it is a commercial one and it has been consistently held that in order to determine its value, the value must be determined on a particular date. [321E F] 1:3 In the instant case, the assessee had maintained its books of account in accordance with cash system of accounts adopted by it during that "previous year" stop there. The method adopted by him is not only a collection but also realisation of moneys which are ultimately earned on accrual. It was apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be include within the assets of the an assessee under the Wealth ' Tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts were maintained on Cash basis interest due on accrual base, though not realised, on the Outstandings from the money lent business are liable to included in its net wealth of the assesee. [313C D; 313A B] Commissioner of Wealth Tax, A.P. I vs M/s. Vysyaaraju B Cadreenarayana (Orissa) (1), and Commissioner of Income tax, A P.I. vs Kigolla Narasimha Rao, ; , referred to. 1:4 The scheme of the wealth Tax Act is that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last date of the "previous years", as the valuation date. The figure of net assets of assessee at the end of the 'previous year ' takes into account the financial activities of the business during that 'previous Year" takes into consideration the financial activity of the asscssee during that previous year. It does not appear that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by assessee.

The respondent was a civilian employee of the Central Administrative Tribunal. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed certain misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Tribunal for quashing the order of dismissal and also for reinstatement in service. The Tribunal held that the respondent failed to establish his case and accordingly quashed the order. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has no jurisdiction if the findings of the Tribunal are "unreasonable" and not warranted by the facts and circu mstances of the case. [33E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had ma de his choice of forum and was even otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules which are undispu t edly applicable to him. Therefore, if the order may be supported on a finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the 30 punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in imposing the penalty. [34F G] 1:3 In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of the aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the Tribu nal imposes a lesser penalty on the respond ent cannot, therefore, be sustained. [35B C] State of Orissa vs Bidyabhushan Mohapatra, ; , referred to. 1.4 In the case of proceedings transferr ed to the Tribunal from a civil court or High Court, the Tribun al has the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers which a government servant who is aggriev ed by the penalty imposed can agitate in appeal, revision or review as the case may be. [36F G]. 1:5 In the present case, since the respondent has ma de hi choice of proceeding and was only otherwise dealt wi th the Government servants (Conduct), Rules which were undispu s tedly applicable t he respondent was one which reasonab le person would draw from the proved facts of the ease, t he High Court cannot sit as a court of appeal over a decision based on it. [37F G; 38A] 1 :6 In the absence of any finding as regards substantial misdemeanor for which punishment can be imposed and if t he conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter, the High Court could not sit as an appellate court over a decisi on based on such evidence. [38C] State Of Orissa vs B.K. Das, ; ; State of U.P. vs Bidhyabhusan Mohapatra, , referred tO.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 1. He claimed to be a lessee under section 4(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief in respect of the property in question. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit was barred by res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the trial court had no jurisdiction to decide the question of status as lessee against the plaintiff and that the decision of the Mamlatdar was not final on merits. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by section 58(2), from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1032C] 1.2 In the instant case, the decision in the earlier suit was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former Suit and hence it was not open to the Civil Court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of the agricultural land. If, on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, the Civil court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [1133D] 1:3 The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Act and section 58 (2) specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any matter which is required to he settled, determined or dealt with under the statute. Therefore, the question whether defendant No1 was a tenant in respect thereof should be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil Judge if the issue is held against defendant No 1, the civil Court may consider passing of a decree in eviction but if on the facts it is found that defendant No,1 was not a trespasser, the suit for possession would have to be dismissed because it would not be open to him to give relief to him by way Of possession of agricultural land.[1133E F] 1 :4 The jurisdiction under section 58 is vested in Mamlatdar under Section 7 of Act and Section 58(3) specifically prohibits the Civil Courts from settling or dealing With any question whether a person is a tenant or deemed tenant.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they seek enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". The petitioners want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They want the said pay scale of the regularly employed carpent er and painters and carpentors ' helpers engaged in the construction industry. They have also sought enforcement of the right to equal pay for Equal work. The Corporation has clearly stated that there are no regular employees of the petitioners ' categories in its establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. The Court pointed out that principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The court pointed out, that principle had to be interpreted into Article 15 of the Consti tution which enjoins that equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. It is important to emphasize that equal work for equal Work is a concomitant of Article 14 Of the Constitution. From the averments in the pleadings of the parties it will be clear that the Corporation has no regularly employed engaged carpent ers. The principal claim of the peti tioners therefore fails and is rejected. [669F H] Randhir Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed.

The prosecution case against the accused was that on or about 29th November 1975 at about 6 p.m., the deceased and his wife were returning home from their village after taking meals in the fields of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and the accused 1 to 3 armed with deadly weapons, entered into a conspiracy for murder of Malan and his daughter. The deceased was returning home on the way to the village where the accused 2 and 4 were standing. On the way, the deceased came out of the village and started running away from the village. The accused 1 and 6 were armed with sticks, spears and sticks. They attacked Malan with sticks and sticks and caused injuries to them. The prosecution case was that the accused No. 1 and 2 had entered into an agreement for the purchase of a plot of land in the village for construction of a house on the same day. On or about 30th November, 1975 at 6 p P.M., the accused along with his wife and children went to the fields where Malan was standing. The complainant party reached the field and saw Malan coming out of his house and the deceased lying in the field. At that time Malan came out from the field with a gun and fired at him. The other accused were armed by sticks, sticks and iron rods. They also attacked Malin with sticks. The defence version was that they had entered the agreement for sale of land on the date of the agreement and that the deceased had been assaulted by the accused persons. The trial court acquitted all the seven accused but convicted them under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced each of them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 304 Part 1 read with Section 34 I P.C., and also under section 120B I. P. C. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to the accused. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that (1) the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under section302 read with s 34 IP. C.; (2) the confession of the accused 5 was not recorded in accordance with law and (3) the conviction of accused 1 under section 300 read with 149 I.p.C.; and (4) the confirmation of the conviction by the trial court under section 306 read with S.34 I.A. could not therefore be sustained. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused 2 to 4 could not have been relied upon in this case in view Of the fact the accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquittal by the Trial Court under section 307 read with 34 I .P.c., and accused 5 alone was a party to the conspiracy the conviction Of accused 5 only of the charges framed against him under section 148 read with sections 120B, I.I.P., could be sustained.[138D] 2. The confession of Accused 5 could have been used against accused 6 in view the fact he had not filed any appeal in this Court against his acquittal and also the fact of that accused 5 who was not a party in charge No.4 which was framed only against accused 1, 6 and 7. [139E F] 3. The conviction of Accused 2 alone could be upheld. [140G] 4. The last part of section 34 is that if an offence is committed by any person other than the accused, he shall be liable for such offence in respect of which he is charged or to be tried and punished under this Act. [141B] 5.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) and his two sons, filed a suit for the execution of the will alleging that after the death of Sadagopalachar, her husband Narayana lyengar became the absolute owner of all the properties and so Lakshmma was not competent in law to make a will in respect of any of them. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to establish that when Lakshmamamma was alleged to be executed the will she was in sound and disposing state of mind, that it represented her intentions. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that even if it had found in favour of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that he had really understood its contents, had approved of them and had put her signature on it when she was In a sound disposing state. Held, that the onus of proving the signature of the testatrix on the will raised a presumption that the will had been executed was upon the propounder to prove his execution. The onus was not discharged by the appellant in this case. The burden of establishing the signature on the instrument was on the propounder and it would be difficult to treat the evidence of this witness as suffi cient to prove that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the document before she put her signatures to the will.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arcons, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by it. The use to which they are generally put, showed that the expression "electrical goods" meant for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The Sales Tax authorities rejected their claim on the ground that they fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant 's revision application before the High Court was dismissed by a Single Judge who held that the use which is generally made of the arc carbons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the word "electric goods" to describe them, suggesting a connection with electricity, and their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electral goods" as contemplated by the entry in the Madras Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the entry does not include parts of motor vehicles. [562B] The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that electric motors under consideration are covered by the relevant entry No, 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales tax Act. Neither the use of the term "electricity" to describing them, suggests a connection between electricity and their utilization in projectorors in Cinemas. [563C D] The word "accessory" is employed in several entries such as entry No,. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for using a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article, manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of apparatus would not cease to be covered by that intended entry simply because a purchaser makes some other use of it.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment had to be used only for minerals development and could not be used for any other purpose sanctioned by law. Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification was in violation of clause(b)of Article 304. [419G] 1.2 The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used merely for development of minerals and not for other pur pose sanctioned by Law. [416B] 1:3 The Act was passed for the development of mineral, but when discharging its function relating to Development, if t he State incidentally allowed mining to he carried on In the public interests and levies, in that connec tion a tax it does no mean that such tax should not be use ed only for development purposes sanctioned by the law. [414C] 1 :4 The fact that section 15 of the Act does no authorise the State Government to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to confer on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the statute under which the rules are made. [413D] 1 5. The fact, that section 17 of the Gujarat Act does not authorise the state Government to showing such concession when promulgating it is a part of sub ordi nated legislation is equally of no consequences. No implied power need be conferred on such delegated authority in the order to do so under order to enable it to act in conformity with the policy underlying the Act under which it was made. The State Government cannot show such a concession while legislating the rules which are not in the character of subordination or conclu sion legislation is therefore, of no avail.

The appellant was the hereditary trustee of a temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the Temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the office of the appellant is hereditary within the expression "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. [445 D] (2) The word 'office ' is used in contradistinction to a mere office which may not have been expressly provided for by the founder. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [427 E] (3) The appellant must therefore be held entitled to succeed.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and also observed that necessarily no case would lie on this kind of testimony against even the absconding accused. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the High Court erred in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of a single witness; (2) the evidence of PW 4 is not corroborated by the contents of the FIR; and (3) the medical evidence does not support the prosecution case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence of this solitary eye witness is not reliable. It is only possible that the court should be circumspect and closely scrutinise the evidence to come to an unhesitating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. [712 D] 2. The testimony of PW4 in cross examination that when he went near his deceased elder brother about hundred persons were there and "none of them asked him as to how it had happened" appears to be contradicted by the medical evi dence. Another very serious departure from his earlier version is that while PW 4 had stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this later version appears to he contradicted by his evidence. Another highly serious departure From his earlier statement is that when PW 4 went near the place of occurrence a little earlier than PW 4, did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. It also stands to reason that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4 who arrived at the place a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. There is considerable doubt as to this testimony with regard regard to seeing the accused running away from the place where he was sleeping to the place when he fell dead. [ 712 E G] 3. The fact that the witness has stated in his first information Report that the appellant was only mention ed the name 'of accused Karunakarhan as his assailants, does not mean that his earlier versions in the FIR stand contradicted by PW 4. If the statement of PW 5 is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the scene of occurrence already when he arrived. It may also be conceivable that those person who gathered will not ask him PW 4 for information With regard to see the accused ran away from tho place where they were sleeping to his place where PW 4 was lying.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased. The income was received by the heirs, legal representatives after his death but in that previous year he died. The Income tax Officer found that the respondents had received the salary due to her husband and that the amount was liable to tax under section 24B(1) of the Income tax Act. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In reference, the High Court held that on a correct interpretation of section 24 B the amounts which were received by them before his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to income tax under s.24B(2). Held, that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the previous year. The fiction is confined to the case provided in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 23B. In the present case the fiction was limited to those cases provided by the three sub sections of section 25B and could not be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. Commissioner of Income tax vs Shaw Wallace & Co., (1932) L.R. 59 I.A. 206, referred to. The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs andlegal representatives after their death they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have be liable when the income was receive had he been living.

The petitioners who were members of the Telengana region, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957. The main contention was that article 16(3) of the Constitution is ultra vires the Constitution and that the State Legislature has no power to make any law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. Held, that the word 'under any State specified in the First Schedule or any local or other authority within its territory any requirement as regards residence within that State or Union territory prior to appointment or appointment to an office in that State is not restricted to residence within the State or any Union territory. The words "any requirement" and "any provision as to residential accommodation" in article 35(a) of 'the Constitution are wide enough to include both residence and residence. The word "under any state" means a whole State as the venue for residential qualification and it is impossible to think that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used such as "any requirements as to resident within that part of the State". The word 'at any state ' means a part or whole State which is the venue of residential qualification. The expression "at any place" in the clause includes both residence as well as residence. It is not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid or not.

The appellant was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them also for offences tinder sections 467 and 471 of the I.P.C., and also for offence under sections 467 & 471 of I. P.C. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him on the ground that he had secreted the articles from his house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father and of which the key was furnished by the father. On appeal, the High Court held that though the locked almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be presumed that he was in possession of these articles. Held, that the prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. The fact that an officer of the post office having in the course of his duties access to postal articles kept or lying in the post offices, the legislature had deliberately enlarged the scope of section 52 so as to encompass secretion, destruction or throwing away of postal articles by an officer even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the are riot articles with which he is required or is competent to deal in the. course of their duties. The mere fact that the locked receptacle contained a small number of items belonging to his father cannot be regarded as being in the joint possession of himself and his father because he had an opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession would be arguing in a circle.

The appellants were convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the Sarpanch had admitted in his deposition that he had to authority to tell Mahabir that his affidavit was not proper because it did not fully evidence the fact that the High Court had passed an order staying proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) It is well settled that contempt of Court is a serious matter and a High Court should be chary of finding a judicial officer guilty of contempt for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the order of the High court. [119 E F] (ii) The High Courts have not kept in mind the principles which we have mentioned above. In certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial Officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of the court. Contempt of Court of Court, is a grave matter and serious matter. [120 E F; 121 A B] (iii) The application did not contain the date of the application. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the applica tion before him. It could not be said, that he bad committed contempt because a Court is entitled not to act on an application which is not accompanied by an affidavit properly sworn to or certified copy of the orders He has committed criminal contempt of courts for disobeyed its orders if there is no unimpeachable evidence, that the Judicial officer had know of the dismissal of the petition. [122 E F].

The appellant was charged with murder and was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge, Etawah, for having committed the murder of Sheo Sahai. The High Court dismissed his appeal and confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai or not, as he was of opinion that the prosecution case against him was insufficient. Held: (i) The extra judicial confession of an accused to a police officer is admissible in evidence under section 24 Of the Evidence Act and it must be proved by clear and unambiguous evidence of the fact that the accused person who committed the crime had no motive for committing the murder, [209 E] (ii)The statement made by the witness at the Police Station is admissible under section 25 Of the Indian Evidence Act. The extrajudicial confession of a person to a Magistrate or a police Officer in pursuance of an enmity arising out of minor disputes, would be admissible in proof of his guilt unless it is corroborated by other evidence. [209 G H] (iii)The High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered the deceased and was, thereafter having a bath. The confession of his co accused to Ujagar Singh does not amount to an confession of any offence under section 27 Of the Act.

The appellant, a voter of the Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls) Rules 1963, framed under the Madhya Pradesh Munichian Corporation Act, 1961, was declared elected to the Madhya Bharat Legislative Assembly on December 31, 1978. The election of the appellants was challenged by two candidates who had not been included in the electoral roll. The High Court dismissed their petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the said notice before Shri K. C. Sharma, Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the entire electoral process had been vitiated on the account of non compliance with Rule 4 (3) of Madhya Pradesh State Municia 493 pal Corporation Act; and (ii) the declaration of results of all the successful candidates was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners were entitled to issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored. [44E] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioners had not filed any claim to include his name in the Electoral Roll on October 19, 1978 more than two months before the date on which i was filed. It is difficult to place any reliance on the said news item for the purposes of concluding that the Collector, Raipur had been informed about the defect. [45F] 2:2 The petitioners had also not filed a claim to inclusion in the roll on October 20, 1978 and that was rejected by the Deputy Collector after following the prescribed procedure prescribed under Rule 8 of the Madhya pradesh Munichinjamunici Singh Corporation Act. [46G H] 3.1 It is not the case of the petitioners that they did not know immediately after the publication of such notice that in the said notices a period Of 20 days had been mentioned in its preamble as the period within which the claims and/or objections could be preferred and in paragraph 7 thereof it had been stated that any such claim or objection filed beyond the prescribed period was liable t to be rejected. [47A] 3:2 It is also not the contention of the respondents that they were entitled for the issue of a writ prayed as of rights. The writ petition itself was presented on December 28, 1978 for the first time that the attention of the Collector was drawn to the said error and that the writ petition alone was presented in December 1979. [48B] 3 :3 It is impossible to place an reliance on this news item because it was only on December S, 1978 that the reference could be filed on and after November 25, 1978, for the second time that a period had been specified in its Preamble as the periods within which claims and objection could be made and in Paragraph 7 thereof. [49C] 4:4 The petitioners are entitled to the issue Of the writ sought for as right and delay in making the petition. [50E] 5:5 In the circumstances of the case, it is difficult that any reliance was placed on the news item dated December 28 1978 for concluding that it was merely on December 27, 1978 which was filed on December 29, 1978 by the petitioners. The Writ Petition itself was filed in December, 1979 and therefore, the writ Petition itself had been presented on 12th December, 1980.

The first respondent company was incorporated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The company had its registered office at Madras and its registered offices were situated within the limits of the State. In the year 1967, the company closed down its business and started functioning as a stockist under the name and style of "M/s. Vulcan Industries (P) Ltd., Madras. On October 30, 1967, it was found that the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section, was not laid before a general body, but copies thereof were forwarded to the Registrar of Companies for being filed with the Registrar. The first respondent Company filed a complaint against the appellants and its directors for failure to Me with the requisite Registrar of companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, which is alleged to have been committed by them in violation of section 220. The appellants contended that the complaint was barred by limitation as the period of limitation had expired on October 30. 1967. The trial court dismissed the complaint holding that the complaints were barred by time and that the limitation had not expired on the date of filing of the complaint. On appeal, the High Court held that if no balance sheet is laid before the general body there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 221 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balancesheet and profit account before the company may expose it to punishment udder under other provision of the Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . In this Court, HELD : (1) The view taken by the High Courts that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134 of the 1913 Act is correct. [437 B] (2) The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meetings. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit or loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, have been laid before it three copies thereof shall be filed with Registrar. If no balance sheets are laid before any general body the same cannot be heard to say in defence to the charges brought against him that because the general meeting had not been called, the balance Sheet and profit loss account could not be laid before them. [414 G H] (3)(a) The words "in default" occurring in section 134(4) of Companies Act are wide enough to include within its scope a continuing offence also. [416 A B] In the instant case, on principle and authority it should be held that no offences were committed by directors in the present case under sections 134 and 220 of Companies ' Act, and section 220 was not applicable. [420 C D] (b) The word "shall" used in section 135(4), does not mean a mere irregularity or mistake but a mere error or omission to do something which is not within its contemplation. It is clear therefore that on principle the decision must necessarily lead to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section134 of the Old Companies Act and section 221 of the Indian Companies Act the company and its Directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general Body meeting as a defence to them.

The respondents were convicted by the Special Court under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, for having committed offences punishable under sections 5(2), 5(3) and 5(4) of that Act. The High Court held that although the need for a speedier trial was desirable in the disposal of all offences or classes of cases, speedi er trial could be assigned by it to the Special court. Held, that the classification made by the impugned Act was not reasonable and did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. It was well settled that the object of the Act was to provide for speediers trial of certain offences and to make them more expeditious, and that the Act did not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to the trial of any offence or classes thereof. The classification made was reasonable and it was not necessary to ascertain whether it was actually based on such a classification. It could not be said that the impugned legislation was violative of article 14 Of the Constitution as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial such offences or class of cases or classes or classes, and if any charge of discrimination can be levelled at all, it can be made only against the act of the executive authority if the Act is misused. The object being, as I have said, different ele ments, it follows that the purpose by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences or the cases, for in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of offences from another offence, or class or of cases speedie trial is desirable in disposal of All offences or Class of cases.

The appellant was appointed as Radiologist cum Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in the Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He continued to hold the post of Radiologist in the said hospital till 1974 when he was promoted as Radiology cum Associate professor of Radiological (ex officio) in the Medical Colleges and treated as an Associate Professor. The appellant 's claim for promotion to the post was rejected by the Government on the ground that he did not possess at least five years teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant holding that the appellant possessed the qualification and experience requisite for appointment to the posts of Associate Professor as he had the essential educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the post in the Irwin Hospital which is a teaching hospital attached to the Ma ul Azad Medical college. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The designation of the appellant as a Radiologist Cum Associate Professor in Radiotheology (executive) in Maulana Asian Medical College is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor or Assistant Professor in a Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and the mere designation of his appellant as such does not give him a right to hold that the post he has been substantively appointed to the said post of Associate professor. [8A B] 2. The status of the Associate Professor (ex Officio) which the appellant holds in the Ultrason Hospital is akin, to that as honorary Professor/ Associate Professor, in the Willing does not confer him a Right to hold his post of Professor of radiotherapy. By parity of reasoning, it is urged that the designation of appellant as Radiological cum Associate Professors of Radiology (Ex officio) by the University of Delhi does not given him a power to hold or to hold any the post or to appoint Assistant Professors and Lecturer respectively in the Specialists ' Grade II for a non teaching job. [884C D] 3. The position which the Appellant enjoys as Radiologists cum Associate Dean of Radiography (exhibit officio) is akin also to that in honorary Professor and Associate Professor/Assistant Professors in the willing donomjang hospital or the Hospital and mere designation does not make him eligible for appointment. [874C E] 4. The post of Assistant Professor of Pathology ( ex officio) which was a teaching post, was a clinical post while that of Associate Dean was a Teaching post. That being so, it was urged that there is a distinction between the two posts of Radiologists and Associate Professors as the post which the appellants hold in the Colonial Medicine and Surgery. The mere designation or the appellant 'as such does cannot give him any right to holding the Post of Assistant Professors of radiological, nor can he be considered eligible for promotion or appointment. By analogy, it would be difficult to support the impugned action of the Government of India in the Health Ministry in holding that teaching experience gained by the Appellant as Radiographer cum Associate Director of Radiographic (ex officio) with effect from October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into consideration. [864D E] 5. The question whether a Specialist Grade II in a teaching institution belonging to the Central Government is eligible for being considered for appointment or promotion as a Professor of pathology under r. (2) of the Central Civil Health Service Rules, 1963, as amended by the Central health Service ( Amendment) Rules 1966, and if not, whether the appellant is eligible to be considered for such appointment or appointment, is a question which has to be determined in accordance with law. [854E] 6.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The first and the main point argued was that casual workers should also be paid minimum wages on the same basis as the permanent workers for whom the minimum wage was fixed by the Tribunal which is being varied by this Court. On behalf of the workmen it was contended that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in fixing the minimum wages in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wage prevailing in other industries in that region which, in its opinion, would be appropriate under the circumstances of the case to fix the minimum rate of wages in those industries. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and, at the time of reference at least there was not and there could possibly be a claim for higher bonus on the ground that, under the Agreement of 1959, the workmen and the Company had agreed specifically to exclude these classes of workers in regard to payment of bonus. [678 F] (ii) The principle which is applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months basic wage in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account. [682 G H] French Motor Car Co., Ltd. vs Its Workmen, ; , followed. (iii) In the Aluminium Factory, the number of workmen who have to be paid production bonus is very small and almost insignificant as compared with the number in the company 'In these circumstances, it would be more appropriate to compare the total wage packet of the Company with the wage packet received by the workmen of other industries. [679 G H; 678 A B] (iv) The claim was based on the circumstance that according to the workmen, the bonus in their case was being calculated as equivalent to three months ' basic wages, while, the case of some clerical staff, the calculation was made on the assumption that it would have to he taken into consideration.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 19 19. The Income tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, calling upon the assessee to furnish within 30 days from the date of service of the notice a return of his income or the income of such other person during the previous year, in the prescribed form and verified in the manner and setting forth such other particulars as may be prescribed. The assessee did not file any return under section 139 for the said assessment year. The Commissioner issued a notice to the assessee under section 147(2) of the Act on June 3, 1966. The material portion of that notice reads as follows "Notice under section 149 of the Income tax 1961. Whereas (1) have reason to believe that your income chargeable to tax for that year has escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147 of the I.T. Act,1961, and (2) have reasons to believe (i) that you are assessable to tax in respect of which you are liable to pay tax under the provisions of the . . ". The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice on the ground that it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i)(a) The Commissioner was not satisfied that the assessee had made out any reason for coming to the conclusion that the income chargeable under the Act had escaped assessment for that assessment year; nor could it be said that he as a consequence of information in his possession, had reasons to belief that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of these assessee to make a return under s. 139 for any assessment year to the Income Tax Officer or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for the accounting year in question, income chargeable has escaped assess for that years; nor did it be stated that he was satisfied that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice under s 148. [444 B C] (b) The report submitted by the Incometax Officer to the Commissioner is not vague and indefinite. He does not himself record that he had been satisfied that there was no reason for him coming to his conclusion on the material before him that this is a fit one for issue of notice under S 148. The report made by the Incometax Officer to Commissioner, it is clear that he could not have had reasons in believe that by virtue of information contained in his own possession, the income charged to tax has escaped. [445 D] (c) Section 151(1) does not say that the Income. tax Officer is satisfied that it is a case for issue or notice under. 148. He did not himself recorded that he is satisfied whether this was fit case to issue notice under Section 148. In the present case, if only he had read the report carefully, he could never have come to the conclu sion on the materials before him.

The appellant was a firm carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of goods. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the firm for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim holding that there was discontinuance of the business at the date of partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the appellant, the Tribunal held that as a result of splitting up there was a discontinuance of its original business at that date and on the discontinuance of it the family ceased to exist and its business was carried on thereafter by two independent firms for the document of October 30, 1943, and that the income, profits and gains of the previous year shall be deemed to have been the income. profits and losses of the earlier years were not liable to tax under section 26(2) of Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. The High Court on reference held in favour of the appellant. Held:(i) that the business must have been charged to tax by the Income Tax Officer under the Indian Income tax law, 1918, and if so, to what extent. Sub section (3) and sub section (4) in so far as it is relevant for our purpose are as follows: Sub section 3 of section 25 provides that where any business, profession or vocation on which tax was at any time charged under the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1918 is discontinued, then unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions Of sub section 4 have been rendered applicable no tax shall be payable in respect of the income profits, profits or gains of that period. Sub s.(3) provides that "where any business profession, profession, vocation onwhich tax was charged under this Act is discontinued then unless it has been succession by reason of which such provisions have been made applicable no Tax shall be levied in respect thereof". The effect of the amendment of section 26 (2) is that the liability to pay tax arises when there has actually been a discontinuance. The fact that he was not taken on in the original business also shows that the original firm in respect Of which alone the benefit of section 15(3), and (4), can be claimed, continued uninterrupted. On March 28, 1939, there was no family partition and some vilasams were allotted to the father and the rest to the son, and he was the assessee ' In the assessment year 1939 40, the son claimed that there had been a discontinuation of the original partnership business within the meaning of section 24(2), and claimed the benefit under that sub section on the ground that the firm ceased to be exist and his business was being carried on after April 13, 1938. The income tax Officer rejected this claim holding (i)that the business of the assessee was not liable for tax for the period between April 13 and 1939, and (ii) that there could be no question of succession to the business carried on at the commencement of the Act of 1918, that is, April 1, 1939 and on which income tax was charge under the Act Of 1918. Held, further, that the appellant was not entitled to the benefits of section 23(4), because the change in the constitution of a partnership firm was effected after April 1. The business of a firm is not one of its businesses but one of the businesses which has paid tax under the Income ' tax law of 1918 and it is the business which was taxed under the 1922 Act which must cease to exist before the benefit Of section 25 (3), can he obtained.

The appellant 's husband was the owner of a joint family properties. The suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition. The plaintiff 's father died in 1945 leaving behind his widow, two daughters and the widow. The other three got 1/4th share each. That, in short, is the case of defendant 1. By a judgment dated March 19, 1975 a Division Bench of the High Court dismissed defendant 1 's appeal and allowed the plaintiff ' 's cross objections by holding that the suit properties belong to the Joint family and not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The heirs will get his or her share in the interest which the deceased had at the time of his death, in addition to the share which he or she received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share of the plaintiff in the 1/3rd share is 1/6th. [766 F] (2) The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get a share in his interest which he had at that time, in add to the shares which he would have obtained had there been a partition during his husband ' ' ' life time between him and his two sons. [764 G H] (3) Explanation 1 to section 6 resorts to the simple expedient, undoubtedly fictional, that the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener "shall be deemed" to be the share in property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before his death. [774 A B] (4) The crucial words in Explanation 1 are "the interest of the Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary". The expression "in the property" is not defined in the Act but in the Indian Succession Act, 1956.

The appellants, who were employees of the Corporation, were transferred to the service of the Corpora tion on or after 1st September 1956. The first respondent was appointed directly to Class I post after 1 st September 1956 and he was confirmed in that post by the Corporation in 1965. He was promoted to Class II post on 1st October, 1966. In the year 1965, the appellants were transferred from Class III posts to Class III post. On 1st November, 1966, the first respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of Regulation 19(2) of the Regulations and also the amendment made in the year 1977 by the Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the employees of Class III and Class IV who had entered service of tho Corporation after 1th September 1956 were not entitled to continue in service beyond the age of 58 years on their being promoted to a Class I posts or Class II posts. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that since he had the right to continue to be in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age Of 60 years as a class III employee by virtue of the settlement and the amendment of the regula tion 19 in the years 1965, he could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to the Class I Post. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. Regulation 19 (2) is not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees or employees appointed after 1.9. 1956 by virtue Of the settlement. The amendment made by the new sub regulation (2), of regulation 19, empowered the appointing authority to extend at its discretion the service for one year at a time upto 60 years of age. [223D E] 2. Regulation 18(2), however, does not deal with the question whether the age or retirement of employees who have joined the service after 1 9 1956 should be raised to 60 years. On a careful consideration of all the aspects of the case it is felt that the High court erred in striking down regulation 19(1) as amended in the Year 1977, and in directing the Corporation to continue the 1st Respondent in its service till he completed the ageof 60 years on his being promoted as Class I employee by reason of the Settlement and the amend ment of the regulations in the manner indicated therein. [225F G] 3. Regulation 20(2)(a) deals with premature retirement of an employee belonging to Class 11 or Class III category appointed to the serv ice of the corporation on or before 1st Septem ber, 1956 for one month at a place upto 60 year of age and at any time thereafter on giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The proviso thereto makes it clear that the appointing authori ty may extend his service for two years at a suitable place upto sixty years of the age. The modification made by this sub regulation is not to be treated as an amendment of Regulation 20 but only clarificatory and does not affect the effect of the amendment. [226B C] 4. Regulation 21(2A) deals only with premature retire ment of employees belonging to class 11 or class II categories appointed to Class 111 posts on or prior to 1st Decem ber 1956. It is not a case where the employees who had joined service of Corporation after January 1, 1966 were entitled to remain in service upto 60th years of 58, but they had been appointed subsequent to 1 9 1966 by the corporation in respect of whom the Corporation has fixed the age for retirement as 58 years which corre sponds to the age and retirement in almost all the public sector establishments, the Central Government services and the State Government serv ice. [227C D] 5.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial aloofness of a Judge. The appellants were convicted under section 120B read with section 109, I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years each. On appeal by special leave it was contended that (1) the contents of the letter which he and others addressed to the Governor of Punjab and Haryana High Court cannot be construed as scandalising the Hon`ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice; (2) the allegations in the letter were vague, indefinite and indefinite; (3) the letters did not constitute contempt. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The High Court was right in accepting the apology without finding that the appellants committed any contempt. [246E] (b) The matter did not form any contempt because of the fact that the High Court proceeded on the basis that the allegations were unchallenged. [245F] (c) The letter in question was addressed by the deponent to the appellant and said "on a perusal of the contents thereof a prima facie case contempt is made out". The High court did not mention which particular portion of the letters constituted contempt of court. It is no part of duty of a judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a Court to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. [244E] 2(a). In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communica tion in question is brought personally by two members of the Bar Association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a closed cover addressed to him for being handed over to him. The deponent most respectfully submits that the contents were not scandalising or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of the learned Judge or of the Hon ble Court or to weakens in any way the confidence of the public in the adminis tration of justice.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. He was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1947 48 on the basis that he had evaded payment of tax on income and had evaded income tax. The petitioner contended that section 5(4) of the Act offended article 14 Of the Constitution as it violated article 20(3)(a). Held, that sub section (4) was not violative of article 19(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitution and was void. Section 5(1) of Act XXX of 1947, which provides for the procedure to be followed by the Commission is in the nature of a proviso to sub section 4 which says that for the purpose of enabling the person whose case or points in whose case is being investigated to rebut any evidence brought on the record against him, he shall, on application made in this behalf and on payment of such fees as may be prescribed by rules, furnish with certified copies of documents, statements, papers and materials brought on record by the commission. The procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as affects the persons proceeded against under that sub s is a piece of discriminatory legislation offends against the provisions of article 14 of the constitution and is thus void and unenforceable. The provisions of section 5 and the procedure prescribed for obtaining information from the Commission are contained in section 7 which provides that subject to the provisions Of this Act, the Commission shall have power to regulate its own procedure and that the powers of the Commission under sub sections (1), (2) (3), (7) and (8) of section 6 and sub sections(2) and 4 of section 7 may be exercised by any member thereof authorised by the Central Government in this respect.

The appellants, a "commercial establishment" carried on in the premises in question. The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (Respondent 1) was formed for the purpose of carrying on business as trade and commerce in the said premises. It had its registered office at Delhi. Its activities were carried on by it with its registered offices at Delhi and Delhi. The appellants ' contention that the activities of the Federation carried on outside the State of Delhi amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary" to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition was rejected by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the activities carried on at the premises were a "trade, business or profession", and (ii) the activity of the Association amounted to 'work in relation to, or ancillary to trade" within the meaning of section 2(j) of the Act which, in consequence had no application. HELD: (i)(a) The definition of "business" given in the Act is far wider than that of " commercial establishment". [321 B] (b) The activity of a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. As regards the preliminary objection it was true that before the High court it was not argued that the activity carried on was a business or trade. But the fact of the matter is that the respondent is a Federation which is mainly engaged in the promotion of its objects and activities. [322 C] (c) The question whether the activity amounted to a "business ' or a "shop" or a commercial establishment, is essentially a question of fact depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not necessary that the particular activity must be carried on with a view to carrying on any business or business. [328 D] (d) The fact that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Union as set out in its Memorandum of Association, and is not distributed among its members. [330 E] (e) The contention that even if this plea was allowed to be raised, then also the primary activity of that Federation cannot, by any stretch of reasoning, be called a " trade" business of profession within the definition of ' commercial establishment ' given in section 2 (j) is not correct because the definition does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the Union also publishers periodicals and issues issues thesame to member Free of this court in R K. of course, it was conceded that before this Court, it had not argued on behalf Of the appellants ' that the undertaking carried on therein was a " commercial Establishment" within section 2.(j) but that the case fell within part (b). [328 G H] (f) The argument that even assuming that this plea is allowed to he raised, it will be only the primary activities of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the purview of a "Shop" and therefore, the main activity of such a Federation cannot be called as a "Trade" business. It would also bear repetition if the definition is read in the context of any particular trade, business of trade or commerce. [325 F G] (g) The mere fact that a member of the association has some interest in the matter does not mean anything by which profit is earned.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in Benaras. The income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that "in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and although the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay the same. The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the assesse was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors were granted in perpetuity a right to one fourth of the land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. It further observed that the income of trust appropriated by the appellant as remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the income appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. The question referred to the High Court was: "Whether on a true interpretation of clause (viii) Of sub section 3 of section4 of the Indian Income tax, 1922, the sum of Rs. 36,396/ received by assessee as an allowance during the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50 is revenue income liable to tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922? " The High court answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the source of his income was clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it was not agricultural income as defined in the Act; (2) the income could not be held to be derived from land within the definition in section 2(1)(a) of Income tax. HELD: (i) The right which was conferred by the letter of July 7 1837 was a right in a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collection after deducting cost of Tahsil establishments. It follows from the decisions of the Privy Council and the judgments of this Court cited above that if it is held in this case that the source was income, the respondent and his ancestors were given an allowance of Rs,. 36,397/ which was not in the right to receive rent or Revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The amount of Rs 36,398/ received as remuneration was not received in cash or kind but was a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the respondent 's predecessor in 1836. [705 C D] (ii) The source and character of income are, therefore, altered when a part of the agricultural income of a trust is appropriated by it as his remuneration, and that is so notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the profits, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. [700 E F] (iii) The income of Rs 26,398 was not exempt from taxation as agricultural income.
