The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the nationalisation of transport services in the State of Karnataka. Section 68 F(1 H) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, an application for stage carriage permit from a State Transport undertaking for operating in any inter State route shall be given preference overall other applications, provided, of course, the authority is satisfied that the State Transport Undertaking would be able to operate in the inter State without detriment to its responsibility for providing efficient and adequate road transport services. Section 47(1) provides for preference to be given to applications for permits from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation, the State Tourist Department and the State tourist Department were not questioned, but the preference provided for by clause (iv) and to be granted to "such operators of tourist cars or such travel agents as may be approved in this behalf by the Ministry dealing in tourism". The proviso to section 63(7) provides a preference to applications from the State transport Undertaking. Section 64 F(I H) prescribes that where, in pursuance of an approved scheme, a State transport undertaking applies for a stage carriage permits, a contract carriage permit or a public carrier 's permit in respect of a notified area or notified route, such permit shall be granted by the State Government in a case where the said area or route lies in more than one region and the Regional Transport Authority in any others. The proviso provides that preference shall be made to applications of all eligible applicants for permits under section 68 F (1 H). Section 68F(I) prescribes a formula for application of stage carriage Permits from the Karnataka State Transport Undertakings, the state Tourism Development Corporations and the Central Tourist Department were also not questioned. The High Court held that the fourth sub clause of the proviso to sec. 63( 7) did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the private operators that the view taken by the High Court and the state Transport Appellate Tribunal was correct and that the fifth sub clause did not violate article 14, since the State Road transport Corporation and the private operator who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63(1), the proper course for the appellant was to set aside the orders of the State 's Tribunal and the High court and to direct the State to hear the appeals and dispose them of in accordance with law, after considering the claims of the eligible applicants in the manner indicated in Sher Singh 's case and now. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a specified notified route or notified area, where under section68 F( I) the permit has to be necessarily granted to the State Undertaking in all other cases, the claims Of all eligible applications must be considered on merits applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1015 A B] 2. The word 'preference ' occurring in Section 47 (1) does not say for example, like section 68F (1), that the permit shall he granted to a State Road Undertaking. What has been said by the Court with reference to the preference to being given under section 47(IH) is unconstitutional and we so declared it. [ 1015 A C] 3. The reservation provided for in Section 63 (7) is valid. It does not mean that the reservation should be made only on an application of a particular individual or of a group of persons who are eligible to apply under section 66(1). [1014 B D] 4.

The respondent, a dealer in the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, was assessed to sales tax for the assessment year 1949 50. The respondent filed an application under r. 21 A of the Rules framed by the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act for recovery of the amount outstanding on the date of default. The appellant contended that the word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (1) is wide enough to include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee, and that the State Legislature had no authority under its rule making power to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. Held, that the respondent was not entitled to recover the amount of sales tax due by the transferor on the one hand and the transferee on the other. The word 'assessable under this Act shall be construed in its widest sense and includes all taxes which are imposed or collected by a dealer. The expression "assessment" is wide and comprehensive enough to cover all kinds of transactions including sales effected before the transfer of the property. The words "assessment " in section 2(1)(c) of Madras General sales Tax Act must be construed as including all other matters incidental thereto. The power conferred on the State by section 19 of the Madras Act is beyond the rule making powers of the State under sections 19(i), (ii) and 19(2)(c).

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra, on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311 (2) and directed that the decree passed by the lower appellate court be varied so as to show that the appellant continued to be in Government service till the date of suit only and there will be a decree for Rs. 1,000/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State of Maharashtra that (1) the High Court erred in holding that there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer before him and (2 ) the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy thereof amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311. HELD : (i) The decree of the High court decreeing payment of arrears of salary is truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. [922 D] (ii) The words 'actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of pay the decree more properly falls under section 60 of the Act rather than under section 61. [936 D] In the present case there was nothing to show what material was influencing the InspectorGeneral of Prisons. The report of Enquiry Officer did not disclose that he had applied his mind to the report and had given his tentative conclusions. The final conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving the plaintiff of a copy. [946 E] (iii) The High court erred in basing its decision on the report submitted by the Enquiring Officer before it and the tentative conclusions arrived reached by the enquiry officer were binding on the State Government.

The appellants, who were the successors in interest of the respondents, made an inquiry and came to know that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached land unworkable. The trial court held that the defendants had encroached on their leasehold land within three years of the date of the filing of the suit, that the suit was not barred by limitation and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. On appeal, the High Court reversed the findings of the trial court and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pit pit in the encroached area; (ii) article 49 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, applied to a suit and the appellant was entitled to relief under article 48. Held:(i) The High Court erred in holding that the burden of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondent beyond the prescribed time was on the appellants. (ii)(a) The onus of proving that he obtained the knowledge of a particular fact within three year of the institution of the action is on the plaintiff and not on the defendant. (b) The appellant gave evidence to show that the encroachment was prior to 1932, but there is no acceptable evidence on their part to establish that the appellants came to knowledge of it only in the year 1941 which was within three months of the said date.

The appellant was a textile mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. On June 25, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The Manager of the Mill went outside and threatened him with physical injury. He then informed Sankaran that in view of his denial a departmental inquiry would be held and he was also placed under suspension pending enquiry. On July 8, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran the same day. In the meantime Sankaran was informed by one of the workmen that in spite of his refusal a departmental enquiry would be conducted and he would also be placed under suspended pending inquiry. On August 10, 1958 Sankaran was intimated that in case of failure to hold an inquiry against him the management would have to take disciplinary action against him. The appellant thereupon filed a petition before the Industrial Tribunal for quashing the order of termination on the ground that it was mala fide and colourable exercise of the power conferred by r. 12(a). The Tribunal held that the action taken under r, 18(b) was bona fide and was not colourable exercise Of the power under that rule. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Industrial Tribunal had the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). [14 C] (ii) In the present case, the tribunal held that it could not be said that view was incorrect. The employer could defend the action under r., 18(c) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was taken under rule 18(d). [15 D] (iii) In a case of this kind, the requirement of bona fides is essential and if the terminaton of service is a colourable exercise it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination.

The appellants filed a suit for declaration that the agreement dated December 1, 1960 was not a lease. The trial court held that the consent decree operated as res judicata and that the document dated November 27, 1954 was not of the nature of a lease; that in view of the consent decrees the defendants 5 and 6 were estopped from contending and leading any evidence and putting questions in cross examination of plaintiffs witnesses to show that the said document dated December. 1,1960 was not lease; and that it was not even averred that the rights granted were in the nature Of leasehold rights; that the suit was for declaration of the rights of Filmistan to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre under the agreement of November 27 1954, and for an injunction restraining the defendants from violating the said rights of the Filmisten under the said agreement. The Trial Court held that it had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the character of a 'lease ' within the meaning of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act; that it did not relate to a matter to be decided by the Court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant. The High Court, however, held that in respect of the terms of the said consent decree as also of the agreement the defendants Nos. 5 and 7 were estopped and leading evidence and put questions in crossexamination of plaintiffs ' witnesses to prove that the aforesaid document dated October 27,1954 was not an lease; but it further confirmed the document on December 1 1960, and further confirmed by document dated January 31, 1955 and further affirmed by document on January 31. 1960. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question whether in fact the subordinate court has decided the question of res judicata or whether the consent order operated as a res judicata is not vested in it by law. [475 E] (2) It was not decided in Major section Khanna 's case that every order of the Court in the course of a suit amounts to a case decided. If the court adjudicates for the purposes of the suit some right or obligation of the parties in controversy; every order in the suit cannot be regarded as a case deciding within the scope of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [441 G] (3) The consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 had not been decided that it related to a matters to be determined by the court and on that account the consent judgment in suit no. 149 was not res judicata.

The respondent, a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a Pilor Officer. In the year 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State also adopted the same scheme. Again the term was extended upto 30th August 1985 by an order dated 1st June 1983. " It is thus seen that the appointment of the respondent was indisputably in the nature of contract and under the last order of appointment refened to above he was entitled to continue in office in the post in question till 30th of August, 1985 and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The respondent aggrieved by the said order filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was enti tled to be reinstated in service on the pronouncement of the Judgment on 24.3.1988 notwithstanding the fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th September, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and directed the appellant State to consider the claim of the respond ent for continu ation in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the High court, the appellants have preferred this appeal after obtaining special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order dated 26th July 1988 passed by High Court on review and restore the Judgment dated 24. 3.1988 passed in the Writ petition are liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. His only case was that the interim order that had been granted by the High Courts during the pendency of the Writ Petitions on 10th July, 1986 entitled him to be re instated in service even though there was no order of extension of service. If the respondent had really aggrieved by his Judgment dated 25th March 1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that fact did not affect in any way what the High COurt has stated in the penultimate paragraph of the judgment dated 24th March, 1988 which reads thus: "It is open for the opposite parties to conider the claim for the petitioner for continua tion in service/ or of Fresh appointment and nothing more. The petitioner proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be reinstatement in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th November 1985. This was not done. The Court, therefore directed that the respondent should be re ried in service within two months from today. [243E F] 2. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the Respondent was entitled ted to be reinstate in service regardless of the merits of the case and the extent of his right.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the acquittal of the appellant but maintained the conviction of the accused. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of P.W. 3 to which was corroborated by the evidence of the doctor who examined the deceased, was not supported by any material or evidence. [368E] 2. The prosecution tried to make P. W. 3 an old woman of 69 years stated in her evidence that she saw the accused who was sitting by the side of the deceased on the cot making a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased and that the deceased cried out 'Amma. The Inspector of Police P. Ws. 1, 2 and 3 had deposed that when there were two divergent versions given by the prosecution and the defence and when two views were possible, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused.[368E F] 3. The doctor who conducted the post mortem examination found the following injuries on the body of the victim: (1) A stab wound over the right side of head with a sharp edged weapon; (2) a incised wound over left side of chest, and (3) a lacerated wound over right side oval region. The Doctor opined that the injury was caused by a blunt weapon. [369G H] 4. The injuries must have been caused in the manner suggested by the defence that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have be upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of thedeceased to send her with him to his house. [370A B] 5. The injury must have had been caused In the manner indicated by the witnesses that is to leave only a remote possibility in his favour, which can be dismissed with the sentence 'of course it is possible but not in the least probable ' the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt, but nothing short of that will suffice. [371C] 6. The nature of injuries received by the deceased could have been inflicted in the way suggested by him. It was obvious that the accused must have were upset by persistent refusal to send his with him at his house and that he had been upset by his persistent refusal. [372E F; 371A B]. 7. The medical evidence did not support the prosecution case. The defence version of the occurrence was one based on circumstantial evidence. The appellant was a Judge of the Madras High Court. He was removed from his office by an order dated 27th May, 1978 passed under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Chief Justice of India in exercise of his powers under section 7(2) of that Act, issued a notice to the appellant on 28th June, 1978 calling upon him to show cause why he should not be prosecuted for an offence punishable under section 5 of the Act and to submit a written explanation within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. The appellant submitted his reply on 30th July, 1978. On 29th August, 1978, the Chief Justice issued a notification under section 4(1) of Act calling upon the appellant to showcause why he be not prosecuted for having committed an offence under section 161 IPC read with section 5(2)(a) and (b) of Prevention of corruption Act, 1988. The notice was received by the appellant in the office of the Chief Judge on 30.8.1978. On 30th August 1978, a notification was issued under section 10(1), which was followed by another notification dated 27.9.1978 calling upon all the members of the staff to show Cause why he shall not be proceeded against for an alleged offence under sections 161 and 165A IPC read along with section 109 IPC. The said notice was served on the appellant by registered post. On 28th September, 1978 a notification u/s 10(2), which provided that no court shall take cognizance of an offence alleged to have been committed by a public servant i.e. the Judge of a High Court includ ing the Chief Judges as in the present case, except with the previous sanction under clause (c) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his offices. The notification was challenged before the High Court on various grounds including that for the purpose of deciding the question of applicability of the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, the office with reference to which the offence under the Act is alleged to be committed, it is necessary to consider the feasibility of grant of sanction under section6 of the said Act for prosecution of a person holding such an office. The High Court rejected all these contentions and dismissed the petition. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) Section 6(i)(C) of Criminal Procedure is not applicable to the case as the holder of such an offices can be removed from office by the President in accordance with clause (4) of Article 124 of the Constitution; and (ii) for the purposes of deciding whether sanction thereunder can be obtained for prosecution or not. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 18 read with article 124(4) and Article 2 18 of the Constitu tion, under which a Judge can be remove from his Office by an Order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members. [216C D] 1.1 The power of superintendence over the High Courts under Article 124(5) is a special law enacted by the Parliament under Article124(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste and not a member. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that Abhoy Pada was a person belonging to a smaller caste group within the Sunri caste, and not as a member thereof. The Election Tribunal held that Abhaoy Pa was a "unit" within item 40 of the Schedule to the Order and dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had established that the appellant belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with Sunri Caste, and (ii) the evidence did not establish that the Sahas formed a sub caste strictly so called within the "the Sunri" caste of a caste wholly independent of the Suniti caste. HELD: The correct interpretation of item 40 is that it indicates men of the " Sunri castes but not those within that caste who formed the smaller caste groups of Sahas. [391 E] In the present case, the appellant was not a "Unit" and he did not belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 though he was a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to that caste. The evidence clearly established that Abhuoy Pas was thinking of that group as consisting of those Sunris who bore the surname Saha. [392 G] In view of the fact that the respondent did not claim that there was within the ' Sunri ' caste, no question of Saha being a distinct class independent of Sunris could arise. L/S5SCI 27 392 If it were right in interpretation of Item 40, then the only question that has to be decided is whether the respondent has established that he belonged to a bigger caste group called Sahas within the expression "excluding Sahas".

The appellant was the tenant of a flat in Bombay. The complainant and his brother went to the appellant 's house for treatment of his failing eye sight and he was found sitting on the ground floor. At that time the appellant asked the complainant to go to the United Kingdom for treatment. On 4 12 1948, the police party who were down below ready for the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 29,500 from the complainant. The police party searched the flat and recovered certain documents. The appellant was charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The Magistrate convicted him under section 13(1) (i) of Act and sentenced him to one month 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs, 500. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condi tion of the relistance by a tenant of his right as such and that in the present case there was no such relinquishment. HELD : (1) The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. The relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of their rights as such. [421 D] (2) The word "relinquishment" was used in the Transfer of Property Act and not in any strict technical sense but in its comprehensive meaning as giving up of possession of the premises; and he pointed out that if it was intended by the legislature that "reltenish ment" should have the limited meaning sought to be placed upon it on behalf of the tenant, the word "surrender" used in section 108 sub clause (i), of the Transfer Of Property Act would have been more appropriate.

The appellant, a Draughtsman in the State of Maharashtra, was appointed as an Assistant Draughtsman on a monthly salary of Rs. 210/ per month. The pay scale of the post of Draughtsman and Rs. 150/ was revised to Rs. 180/ per mensem. The workmen raised industrial disputes before the Industrial Tribunal which held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. On appeal, the High Court set aside the award and directed the Tribunal to revise the pay scale and dearness allowance and there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workman. The appellant contended that the new wage scales had been introduced by way of an incentive to all the employees who were working as Draughtsmen and that the increase in dearness allowance was not justified on account of the fact that the workmen represented by the Union there were several other employees who would also have to be paid, the Tribunal considered it fair. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the appellant that a flat increase to the pay of each individual workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. [176B] 2. The Tribunal was clearly betrayed of a strange confusion in acceptance accepting the contention of the respondent Union that a new wage scale had necessarily to commence with figures Rs. 151/ and Rs 100/ above the existing pay scales. Immediately after the award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was not clearly mentioned in the award that all the employee were to get additional pay of Rs 150/ and that, consequently it fell within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. [177C D] 3. The amendment order required the Tribunal, to revise its scales by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res tructuring the scale of pay and never granted any ad interim increase of salary to all employees. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 200/ and again after the figures Rs 150 / and Rs 50/ was added to the Pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs 150 per month in the case of other categories to the initial pay in the wage scales pertaining to those categories. [179E F] 4. The award of the Industrial tribunal is set aside and the Tribunal directed the appellant Tribunal to give a flat increased salary on Entry into the Service and res pondent No. 1 would be entitled to get Rs.150/ per day from the date of the award, i.e., from the dates when the new scale was introduced.

The appellant, a textile mill, entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded did not amount to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant, to pay the prescribed wages. The authority rejected the appellants ' contention and held that section 15 was applicable to the case because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages before the said definition was amended in 1958. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the terms prescribed by an award could not be included. It is well settled that unlike ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms of contract between the parties when they deal with disputes arising between them in respect of the said terms, industrial adjudication is not bound to uphold the terms Of the contract of employment. If it is shown to the satisfaction of Industrial adjudication that the term of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, it can and often enough it does radically change the terms 'of the contract. The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that on references made under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have constantly been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. The Development of industrial Law during the first decade bears evidence to the effect that on reference made under s 10(l) of Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, terms Of employment had ever been examinedby industrial adjudication.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed certain offences. The trial Magistrate acquitted him on the ground that he had not been able to prove his guilt and that there had been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate. On appeal by the State to the High Court, it held that proof that the thumb impression in the acquittance roll was that of the appel lant was sufficient when taken along with other circumstances to establish his guilt, and accordingly convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. The appellant contended before this Court that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecution under section 196(1), Cr. P.C., had not be obtained under section 198(1). Held: (i) The sanction was necessary under section 195(1)(a) of Cr. The offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery has been brought home to the appellant and he is, therefore, entitled to have it proved beyond doubt that the acts with which the appellant is charged fall within the scope of his duties as a public servant. (ii)The sanction was required under section 199(1); but the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the accused did not claim to have paid the amount to Parma, and the acquit tance roll records the payment, and there is in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. If what appears on the face of the roll is true and whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction then the acts, with which, the appellant was charged fall under the scope oi his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office.

The appellant was a resident of the erstwhile State of Travancore. In 1941 income, profits or gains which a resident made in British India and in the case of Travancore State income, profit or gains arising out of British India or other Indian States were exempted from payment of income tax unless received or brought into the respective territories but this income, income, gains or gains had to be included for the purpose of calculating the rate. The appellant claimed that the loss incurred in the erstwhile Travancore State could not be set off against the business profits made in the former State of Cochin. Held, that the mere use of the words loss of profits or gain to be set aside under section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act did not justify the construction. Section 10 means business in British Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section10 of the Act. The mere fact that the word " income" is not used does not justify a construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India & the Indian States. Commissioner of Income tax vs Shaw Wallace & Co. (L.R. , referred to. The definition of total income " in section 3(1) of the Travancore Act did include business in India or business the profits or losses arising out from British India. Commissioner for Income tax, Bombay City vs Fraser and Sons ([1950] S.C.R., relied on.

The respondent company was a public limited company. Its employees were governed by the Calcutta Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and its employees were entitled to retire at 60 on attaining 55 years of age. The workmen claimed that these showed clearly a tendency in the Bombay region to fix the retirement age at 60 years. The Tribunal found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix retirement age of 58 subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the age for workmen in all industries should be fixed at 60. [445 B] (ii) The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. The reasons given by the High Court for holding that in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in Bombay area the trend has been to fixing the retirement ages at 60, were wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. [427 C] (iii) The decision of this Court on an appeal must be confined to the facts and circumstances of each case. In dealing with a revision application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, it is not necessary for the Tribunal to consider whether the conclusion recorded by this court in some other earlier decisions was correct or not. The Court has also to take into account the fact that in the Calcutta region at least there is a general agree ment that the retirement should be fix at 60 and not at 55.

The appellants were directors of a company which was incorporated in the year 1948. The first respondent, who was one of its directors, was appointed as an Inspector of Companies under section 237(b) of the Central Government. On May 19, 1965 the first respondent passed the impugned order delegating the function of the Board to himself and thereby delegated the function to him by an order dated February 6, 1964 delegating that function to himself. The appellants challenged the validity of the order on the grounds (1) that the order delegates the function under section 236(b), and (2) that it is ultra vires the Central Legislature. Held: (i) that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the appellants was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members and other persons and further that the persons concerned in the management of the affairs of the company had been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and misconduct towards the company and its members. The power conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 237 (b) is administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman of the board by an Order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central government under section 642(1), read with section 10E(5). It may be mentioned that in paragraph 16 of the affidavit the Chairman also stated: "With reference to para 21 of the petition, I have already stated above that there was ample material before the Board on which it could and did form the opinion that there were circumstances suggesting (i ) that the company was being managed with intentto defraud its shareholders, members or any other persons; and (ii) that persons concerned with the management have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect including information relating to the calculation of the commission payable to a managing or other director, the managing agent, secretaries and treasurers or the manager of the Company. The discretion conferred on Central Government by section 239(b)(i) is legislative, that is, it can be validly exercise by the chairman of the general body of directors or any officer of the authority empowered in this behalf. It may also be mentioned in paragraph 17 of the affidavits that there is ample material to show that the affairs were being conducted without intent to evade creditors, member and other person concerned in management of affairs of a Company have been guilty for fraud, mis misfeasance or other misconduct towards its company and their members. It was not correct to say that the Chairman had no power under section 239 (b)(ii) to delegate this function to itself and consequently the company Law Board (Procedure) Rules 1964 made by the central Government on February 1, 1964 and the Chairman 's order of distribution of business dated February June 6,1964 delegating functions of the directors under section 240 to the Chairman are ultra vires.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to two years ' rigorous imprisonment. The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : (i) It must not be forgotton that the offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons or more. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the stolen goods were found in their houses. It may be 723 impossible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.) The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. Even then the time gap is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till suchtime as the old offenders could have taken them away. [723 B C] (ii) The time period of one year and in most cases it is impossible to say that within a short time, these persons were merely receivers of theft property or as receivers of property which was stolen in a dacoity. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of the theft property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence.

The petitioners were manufacturers of 'thinner ' and 'thodox '. They had been importing poisons from the State of Delhi for sale in their factories. The Rules provided that no person shall sell or offer to sell any specified substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. Rule 2(x)(2) of the Rules provides that "no person shall buy, possess or dispose of any specified substances as a poison for purposes of the Act". The petitioners were contending that in substance manufactured by them did not come within Rule 2 (x)(ii) and there were some correspondence in this regard, when the competent authority held that the substance manufactured was 'poisons ' and therefore, they did not question the finding on any material. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale, whether wholesale or retail of poisons and the importation of the thereof. Rules of 1926 were made in exercise of the rule making power under section 3 of the . When this Act 1/1904 was repealed and re enacted as Poison Act 12 of 1919 the definition was omitted and speci fied substances were included in the schedule with a power vested in the State Government to amend the same by Rules including other substances to the list of poems. It is in exercise Of this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old Rule by the following Rule: "13 (1) All poisons kept for sale by any licence holder under these rules (except those kept by a chemist, druggist or compounder for the purchase of dispensing or compounding in compliance with the prescription of medical or veterinary practitioner) shall be kept in a box, almirah, room or building (according to quantity maintained), which shall be secured by lock and key and in which no sub stance shall be placed other than poisons possessed in accordance with a licence granted under the Act, and each poison shall be keep within such box, receptacle or building in a separate closed receptacle of glass, metal or earthenware. (ii) All 'poison ' mentioned in clause (x) of rule 2 shall be retained in a room or a building ( according to quantity maintain ed), which may be secured for by lock & key and In which no substitu tion shall be put other than the poisons, possessed in compliance therewith, almirah or building. " [225D E] 2. The object of the enactment is to regulate sale and the sale, either wholesale or wholesale of poison and the import of the substance as a medicine for purposes o the Act. Rules made under section 4 of the , are intended to control the importation and possession and sell, whether retail or retail. [225F] 3. The purpose of the legislation is to ensure that the possession and dispose of the specified substances are not disturbed by any person who has no absolute right to carry on the same; it is in the exercise of this power rule 13 was amend ed by substituting Rule 2 by the new Rule by substituted the following rule: "2(x) All Poisons kept under a licence holder shall be detained in a suitable receptacle or premises (according as to quantity maintaining), which, shall be secure by lock or key and, in which any sub stance may be placed, other than pseud erary glass, Metal or ear thenware. " The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right on carry ing the same, [225G H] 4. Rule 13 of the rules of 1926 was amended and substituted by the old rule by substituting it the new rule by the words "as poisons" and "pseuder" as "poisoner".

The appellant firm was carrying on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 for referring the following question "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the disallowance of bad debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the assessee in their books of account as irrecoverable was right in law ?" The Tribunal rejected the application but pursuant to an order made by the High Court under section66(2) submitted a statement of the Case on the following questions "Whether the Tribunal was right In law in holding that the debt of the Rs. 1,68385/ due to the appellant was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" Held, that before the question may be answered it is necessary to call for a supplementary statement of case from the Tribunal. The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the appellant to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of its money lending trade nor in respect of any other business of assessee. The amounts sent by, the assessee to the Calcutta firm were neither loans made nor in regard to any other commercial business of that assessee. In view of this finding it is unnecessary to call upon the Tribunal to submit a supplementary Statement of case on the reframed question. The High Court was right. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs Amarchand Sobhachand, [1961] 1 S.C.R. 891, followed.

% The petitioners are owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. Under the provisions Of Section 36 of the Karnataka Act, where the acquisitions, otherwise than by agreement, it will be regulated by the provisions as far as they are applicable, of the Land Acquisition Act. 1894 (the Land Acquisition) Act). The petitioners have obtained interim orders from this Court directing status quo with regard to possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the High Court dated August 14, 1984. On December 16, 1987, two writ petitions were filed by the respective petitioners in the Karnataka High Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards had not been made within the stipulated time. The petitioners also obtained an interim stay from this court directing status Pending further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. In these two writ Petitions, the petitioners sought to challenge the validity of the notifications under Section 4 of the Act and the declaration under section 6 of the Acquisition Act on the grounds that they were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration. The Karnataka High court granted interim stay of further proceedings. On November 29, 1988, the respondents obtained an order from this date directing status status quo as regards possession of lands in Special leave Petition No 294 of1985 preferred against tho order of Karnataka High Courts. In the meantime, the Land Acquisi tion Act was amended by the Bangalore City Improvement Trust (Amendment) Act, 1984 and Section 11 A inserted into the Land, Acquisition Act, 1894 (for short, "the Act"). The petitioners challenged the validity and legality of the declaration on the following grounds: 1. That the awards in these cases had not be made within three years of their publication under section 4 of Land Acquisition (Amendment), 1984; and that as the awards were not ' made within one year of the Notification making the declarations under Section 6 of Land Ac tation Act, the entire proceedings for acqui sition of the land shall lapse. The respondents contended that as they had obtained interim stay orders from the High Courts, the acquisition proceedings had lapsed. That contention was repelled along with certain other contentions in the judgment of the Division Bench of that High Court which is sought to be impugned before this Court. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The petitioners were owners of some lands which had been acquired by them under the Land Act. They obtained interim order from the Karnataka State Government directing status liabili ty quo with respect to possession in Special Appeal No. 823 of 1990 preferred against that order. On September 11, 1985, two Writ Petitions were filed before the High court challenging the acquisi tion on the same ground which was sought to he impugned before the Supreme Court. The said interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [566G H] 1(b) The interim orders had a direct impact on the determination of these Special Leave petitions. It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed.

The workmen entered service of the bank before 1st January 1959 (i) The workman 's basic pay as on January 1, 1959 shall not be reduced in any case. In 1962, the Sastry award provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1. 1962 on stage to stage adjustment basis, i.e., workmen who were drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of the Sastry Award as modified by placing them at the stage in which the Sastry order was made and (ii) the adjusted basic pay arrived at by giving the increments under sub cls. (a),(b) and (c) of cl. (iv) of para 5. The workmen 's scales were revised from time to time by the Sastry Tribunal, but the High Court held that the Sastry awards were not justified in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of paragraph 5.356 of the National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award of June 1962 were inconsistent with the provisions contained in the Sastry Act and the Sastry Awards (Amendment) Act, 1964, which came into force on January Ist, 1959, and that the Desai award was not justified as it was based on a different interpretation of paragraph 516 of the said Sastry Award. HELD: The Sastry Award is not invalid for the reason that it has been made in 1962 and therefore, the provisions relating to revision of pay scales under sub cl. [901 D] (i)(a) The words "in accordance with the Sastry" in para 5 are wide enough to include both the increments provided by sub cls.(a), (b) & (c). [902 F] (ii)(a)(b) The adjustment of basic pay is subject to cl. 10(1) and the basic pay to be fixed on January I, 1959 has to be worked out as on 1st October 1959, the two increments provided in sub cls., (a) &(c) respectively. [992 H] (iii)(b). The words 'in accordance With the Sastry Order are wide and comprehensive enough to cover both the increment provided by subs.(i) and cl. 5. [1003 A B] (iv)(a). The distinction between a "in accord with the terms of reference" and "in pursuance of an award" is that the difference must be in respect of the basic salary as on the date of the reference, i.,e., January 1 1959.

The appellants are the owners of a hotel. They have been carrying on business in the said hotel for several years. The land was leased to the hotel group for the construction of five Star Hotel. The lease deed provided that the land would be allotted to the Taj Group of Hotels for the purpose of constructing a Five Star Hotel, and that the lease would be given to the Zoo logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. The appellants filed an application before the State Government under section 14(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 for permission to sell the land on the ground that the Zo was not run for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres of land proposed to be given for the hotel. The State Government rejected the application and granted permission to the appellants to sell it on the condition that the construction would be made only after obtaining the necessary sanction from the appropriate authority. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority under section 15(2) of West Bengal Act, 1955. The Appellate Authority allowed the appeal holding that the decision to lease the Begumbari land to theZoo was taken on February 12, 1981 and not on February 13, 1981. The High Court also held that the interest and the requirements of the ZO were totally ignored and not kept in mind when the decision was taken to lease it to the Hotel group for construction of a Five star hotel. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government of West West Bengal acted perfectly bona fide in granting the lease of Begumbar land to respondent No. 2. [260F] 1.2 In the face of all these material facts and circumstances brought out by the appellants do not justify an inference that the constructions of the zoo were being made for a particular industry to be set up within the State and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for the purposes. The purpose of the State in such a case is not to earn revenue from sale of resin, but to promote the setting up of industries within the state and invite them for the pur pose. On a consideration of all the facts and circum stances of the case, it is clear that the Government of India acted perfectly bonafide in granting permission to respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to start with, was given to Zoo validly in granting it on condition that they would not be run for any single day unless the essential service which were provided in these four acres had been duly complied with. [261F G] 1:3 The High Courts have rightly held that there was no violation of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the land allotted to respondent 2 was not used for the main purpose of construction of Five Star Hotels. It is true that the State has made available to this Court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the state Government land to Respondent No. 1. The matter was taken in appeal. [262F G; 263A] 2.1 In the instant case, the Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of theZo when they decided to grant four acres to the hotels for the construc tion of a five Star hotel in Calcutta. The object of the Government in such an event is not only to earn profit from sale but to promoting the settingup of industries in the State, and invite these interested to coming up with the necessary pro posal for the ves sion. [263C D] 2:2 In a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of iron and steel products. The assessee had made gifts aggregating Rs. 1 lakh to his son Pravin. In case of entries in the books of account by credit and debit, the sums should be available on the date of gift in the account of the firm whose accounts are said to be credited or debited. The Income Tax Officer included this amount as 'nil ' under section 10(1) (a) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer but the Tribunal held that the sum of Rs.67,560/ was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. In reference to the High Court, the High court held that there was no valid gift on the dates of entries and that the amount could not be included in his property passing on the death of M; and that section 10 did not apply to the gifts of Rs 1 lakh and Rs.50,000 made by the deceased to his wife respectively. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High Courts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee more entries in his accounts in the form would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor and gift in such cases will not be valid. [130E] (2) The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. It was held by the Bombay High Court that there were no valid gifts on the day of entries, then it could not he held that subsequently when the money was transferred by further entries in their accounts, it resulted in a valid gift. [131F] (3) The assessee 's claim for deduction of Rs, 1 lakh from his income under section 12(1)(a) is not sustainable because there was a valid transfer on the relevant date. [132G] (4) The amount of Rs., 1 lakh could not have been included in its property passing to the detriment of the Revenue.

The appellant, a co sharer in the brother 's son of the vendor, purchased certain land from his father. The sale was challenged by the respondents on the ground that it offended the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19 (1)(a) of his Constitution and that there had been no infringement thereof. In appeal, the High Court upheld the constitutional validity of section 15(1) (a) and held that there could be no classification under section 15 which conferred a right of pre emption on the kinsfolk. The appellant contended before this Court that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharers and had not been sold jointly by all the co shar ers, he was entitled to claim the right of preemption under clause 'fourthly ' of section15(1). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The legislature desired to confer the right on specified family members of the vendors or vendors in the first three clauses of section fifteen(1), and with a view to covering all the remaining co shar ers not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses it used the expression 'other co sharants ' in the fourth clause which was meant to serve as a residuary clause to ensure 127 that, no co sharman is left out. [127F G] 2. The Legislature desired to conferment the right to pre empt on specified class family members in the second clause of section 'fourth 'ly ' and with such a view, to covering the remaining land owners not specifically mention the preceding clause it used that the expression "other co particier is left Out" [127G H] 3. The legislative intent was clear and unambiguous. It was not intended to be so construed as to make any distinction between persons who are specified in the erstwhile first three sub clauses of Section 15(i)(b) and those who hold under tenancy of the vendees or vendors who were specified in tho former sub clauses. [128F G; 129A] 4. The expression 'all other co shars ' in clause 'Fourthly ' refers to only those co shar ingers who do not fail under clause "First" or 'Secondly ' or 'Thirdly 'of Section 15 (1) of Act. [129B C] 5. The plain meaning of the expression is that a person who holds under tenan cy of the vendee cannot claim pre ememption but he falls within the expression other co owners jointly. [130C D] 6. The object and purpose of the legislation was to provide for better protection of tenants against exploitation by landlords, tenants and tenants in agricultural lands. It is not intended that a tenant who holds land or property sold or a part thereof cannot claim a pre emation but he must fall within the definition of other coowners jointly. The section does not confer any right on a person to hold land or land which he has inherited from his vendor or vendors. [131E F] 7. The language used in clause "Fourthly" of Section 14(1 ) (a), is wide enough to include all persons who do fail under clauses 'First ' orSecondly" or "Thirdly" and the expression `other co owners ' in cl. (Fourthly) refers to both only those sub sharers who have not failed under clause (First) or 'firstly 'or 'Secondally ' or thirdly ' [132F G, H] 8. The words 'other than co sharing ' in section 15 (i)(a), 'fourthately ' and 'Thirdally ' of Section 16(1A) refer to only such persons who fail under cl. 'Firstly ' as well as 'Second '

The father of the petitioner, who was a minor, filed a suit for title and injunction. The alienees had also filed an application under Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale deeds. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the compromise deed was not genuine and lawful. The High Court in appeal affirmed the decision of the trial court. In the special leave petition, it was contended on behalf of the alienees that the alienation was valid and binding on the alienee respondent No. 2 and that the alienations were valid and the transferees had become owners of the property and had even maintained that there had been improvements of the properties by the alienors. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The compromise deed is genuine and legal and the same has to be acted upon. [540C] 2.1 In view of the fact that there was the allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to the property which too we have not gone into, it cannot be said that the alienes had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and they had even maintain that there has been improvements by the transferees. [541D] 2:2 The alienee has made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to 21.8.1987. The alienation was, therefore, valid and none of the sale deed is valid and no one has any interest in it. The transfereeees have admittedly been in possession of the land from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. [542E] 2 :3 In view thereof, the security furnished in the Trial Court shall stand discharged and the alieners will have no liability to account for mesne profits.

The appellants were the workmen of the respondent company. The company had to pay sick leave for a period of two days only in respect of sickness benefit and sick leave. The Company refused to grant the same on the ground that the company was not entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a, spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The workmen filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and also the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to give the benefit of sick leave to the workmen. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Tribunal erred in not giving the benefit to the company for the second two days sick leave and (2) the workmen did not deserve any more than sickness benefit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1(a) The Tribunal has rightly held that the benefit cannot be claimed as privilege leave as by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. [864 A] (b) It is not necessary for the Tribunal to award the benefit under the Act to award tho benefit of the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in the instant case. The other question regarding the adequacy of the Sick Leave has been examined by the Tribunal with reference to the reports of the National Commission of Labour, 1969, the Labour Laws Review Committee and the Norms Committee of Gujarat State, which go to show that the benefits cannot b.e said to be adequate for, it works out to about half the average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the 1st two days also. [874 B C] (c) The workmen did neither deserve anything more than illness benefit for their first two months of sickness under the first proviso to section 49 of the Act, because, as has been stated, the Tribunal has given the benefit thereof. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege Leave as, by its mere nature, It would be inadmissible only in cases where actual sickness is certified by registered medical practitioners. [884 C D] (d) The contention that what has been awarded by the High court is additional privilege leave for 7 days in the garb of sick Leave, has been rejected by this Court. Such leave could cannot be categorised either as privilege or privilege leave, because it would not be admissible even in the absence of a registered Medical Practitioner. [894 F G] (e) The company was under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefits which the Act allowed for, as had been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit, and does not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. [904 E F] (f) The Company was under an mistaken impression that the sickness concession would be lost for the First two days, of sickness certified as a registered hospital practitioner. It is true that it was not necessary, in the circumstances of the case, to award benefit of 7 days sick Leave with retro modation from January l, 1975, in view of the fact that the Company did not have any medical facilities and the workmen were not entitled for sickness benefits for the third two days. [91 B C; 92 A] 2(a). The Tribunal had rightly held in favour of the workmen, because the Tribunal was under misapprehension that 86 the sickness leave benefit would be loses for the last two days under the second proviso to Section 49 of .

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that he had carried on espionage activities or the details of financial aid received by him from the Portuguese authorities or the names of any of the so called underground workers alleged to have been collected by him or made available by him to the Portuguese Government. The grounds furnished were not specific and no particulars of the activities alleged to be carried on by the appellant were given, viz., the particulars such as the length of period for which the petitioner was alleged to had carried out by the petitioner from the French authorities or names of persons aiding the said petitioner or any details of intelligence alleged to he collected by the petitioning authority. The High Court dismissed his application under article 226 on the grounds that (1) the detaining authority did not disclose the particulars of activities alleged by him and (2) the grounds were vague requiring some clarification. Held, that the right to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. The right of the detenue to be supplied particulars, is subject, subject to limitation under Article 22(5), whereby disclosure is of facts consider to be prejudicial to public interest. The power not to disclose facts considered against public interests cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. If the detenue was furnished information at least to that extent, it will enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right to representation and An obligation to supply cannot be inferred in these circum stances.

The respondent was a member of the Army Staff. He was dismissed from service by the General Court Martial under r. 14 of the Indian Army Rules, 1954. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r.14 of the said Army Rules was ultra vires the . The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order removing him from service. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r 14 of Army Rules 1954, was ultra rites as it contravened article 311(2) (a) of the constitution inasmuch as the respondent had been given the power to dismiss or remove the officer. HELD : The words "subject to the provisions of this Act and such rules" in section 19 of the read with r. 15 of the Defence Rules, 1955, are not ultra vires. Rule 14 is such a rule : it is, therefore, not ultra rites. [446 B] The word 'dismissed ' occurring in section 191 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. [449 C D] In the present case there was no valid rule where under, subject to the other provisions of the Act, the Central Govern ment may remove a man from the serv ice. Rule 15 is such an rule : It is therefore not ultra law. The two sections 19 and 45 of the , are mutually exclusive.

The appellant company imported tea from the respondent Panchayat for consumption, use or sale. The Municipality fixed the rate of octroi on January 14, 1964 and levied octroi duty on that basis. The appellant challenged the validity of r. 3 and 4 on the ground that it was not necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21. Held, that rr. 3 & 4 are not confined to octroi duty only. Rule 5 follows imme diately rr.3 and 4 and is headed "Appeal against levy of any tax or fee". The period of sixty days of limitation commences from the date of the publication of the notice under r .4, i.e., the notice following the decision of a Panchayat to levy any tax, or fee. It follows from this that the Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. Rule 3 and the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the Rules are not restricted to octroi duties only. The scheme of rr. 4 and 5 is headed 'Appeal against the levy of tax or fees".
