The appellant was convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1)(a) of the , and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5 to a Magistrate for having committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a period of six months. The appellants contended that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a long time, further proceedings were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under s 31( 1) of tile Act. Held, that the object of conciliation is to get a settlement made with expedition and therefore under section 12 the Conciliation Officer was bound to make his report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The provisions of the Act are not intended to be exhaustive but only illustrative and general in their amplitude and they cannot be limited to the scope of the enquiry before a conciliation officer or a Board of any proceedings before a Labour Court or National Tribunal under section 10 during the pendency of conciliation proceedings. The Act does not contemplate that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if for some reason the Conciliation officer delays the submission of his report his action (1) ; , referred to in section 12(6) is deemed to take place when the report is received by the Government or when the reference is made to a Court Labour Court, Tribunal or National tribunal under section10 during the course of conciliation proceeding. The words " pendency of such conciliation proceedings" in section 20(2)(b) are wide enough to include all cases which come before a Conciliation Officer or a Labour court and those which come within the scope and purview of the provisions of section 12.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing on 24th December, 1985 on Katras Coal Dump and the petitioner started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish the criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. In those circumstances it appears that the grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. It further appears that after the order of detention was passed and before the actual service of the detention order, the petitioner was taken into custody. From the affidavit of the District Magistrate it does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the detenu or other factors which can justify the detention of a person in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles laid down in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and particularly in the decisions, in Rameshwar Bengal Shaw vs The District Magistrate Etah & Ors., ; , and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate Etah & others, though there was a statement to the effect that the petitioner 's brother and the detenu had been in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. In these circumstances it is not possible to sustain the order passed by the detaining authority under section 2(2). The continued detention of the petitioner under the Act is not justified. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. In the instant case when the actual order of deten tion was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there were such a possibility of release was taken note by the Detaining Authority properly and seriously before the service of detention order. The order of preventive Detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the petition it is nowhere stated that the detenu has since been released or whether the prospect or his imminent release was properly considered by the appropriate authority in the context of the relevant factors. The detention order therefore, is set aside. If however, the detenue is released on bail in the aforesaid criminal cases, the matter of service of order of the deten tion order under the act on the aforesaid materials may be reconsidered by the Appropriate Authority in accordance with law. There will, however, be no orders for release of detenu.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold trade, was carrying on business in gold and silver. The appellant was the owner of the gold firm. The firm had its registered office at Hyderabad. It carried on business as a dealer under the Gold Control Act, 1968. The partners of the firm were doing business in the same premises in which they carried on their business as such dealer. The partnership firm was dissolved by an order dated October 30, 1969 and the firm was granted permission to carry on business of gold and other silver. In pursuance of the said order, the firm had been reconstituted and the partners of that firm were given a licence for carrying on the business of the same firm. On March 31, 1970, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 28 of the Gold (Control) Act,1968 as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969. The High Court struck down the said provision only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to do business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the said premises in Which he carried on trade as such a dealer. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Administrator as is evident from this provision is given unlimited authority or power to refuse to grant permission; and (ii) the section conferred an arbitrary and uncanalised discretion without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The objective, the policy and the scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the statute afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [954C] 2.1 In the instant case, the object of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. In other words, the various restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business are not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry out the business in his licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy & purposes of the act and by the prime consideration that circumvention Of the other provision of the enactment shall not be premitted. [992C D] 2:2 The objective is to ensure, in order to protect the interests of investors, the production, supply and distribution of, use, and possession, of, gold, ornaments and other articles of Gold for matters incidental thereto; and in other words the various provisions of that Act afford more least sufficient guidance. [999E F] 2(a) The policy and purpose of the legislation together with necessity to ensuring prevention of imbalances of circum potency of the various other provisions is to provide, within the economicand financial interests, the control and supervision of the trade in gold ornaments, articles of silver and for matters ancillary thereto. [1001D] 2.(b) The objective of the scheme and the Scheme of the impugned Act together alongwith the necessity for prevention of undue imbalence of circumvenances of the provisions of other provisions are: (i).

The appellants were the trustees of a temple. The properties belonged to the temple and they had been claiming beneficial interest in the property. They claimed that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The trial court held that the lands had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavar by the Carnatic Rulers before the advent of British power in India and that they had acquired title by adverse possession prior to 1 1 1929, and that the appellants were not holding the same as managers of the trust. The lower appellate court found that the new article was not retrospective in operation and that if the title of the alienees in regard to 'dharmadlayam properties had been acquired by adverse Possession prior to January 1, 1929, it would not be affected by the provisions of article 134 B. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question as to whether on facts proved in the present case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed, is a mixed question of fact and law, and the High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title had not been lost by adverse posses sion before the suit was filed. [419 C] (2) The appellants were claiming beneficial interests in the properties all along and that there was no escape from the conclusion that more than 12 years have elapsed since the date of the removal of the previous managers who transferred the properties in question; and so, if a suit were brought by respondents 1 to 3 on the date when they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 1 on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowment, the transfer was void ab initio with the result that the possession had been taken over by other persons who are acting as de facto managers of temple de jure, has not been discussed by the High court. [420 D] (3) The fact that the alienor is still alive, and so it thought that the plea of adverse possi sion could not be sustained. [416 E] Gnanasambanda vs Gnanagambandapu, I.L.R. , referred to.

The respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, was declared to be the sole licensee in respect of a cinema theatre known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu, by the District Magistrate, Jammu (8th defendant) for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as "Apsara Cinema Theatre" and for a prohibitory injunction restraining defendants 1 to 7 from interfering with the running of the Cinema by the plaintiffs and also for a mandatory injunction directing them not to interfere in any manner with the exhibition by the appellants of cinematograph films in the premises of Apsra Theatre. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979. The writ petitioners before the High Court were some of the partners of the firm who wanted to run the Theatre without a licence in contravention of the provisions of the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the licence and answerable to the licensing authority for all commissions and omissions in the Cinema premises, but the writ petitioners did not challenge the order passed by the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was violative of the principles of natural justice in as much as no notice or hearing had been given to the partnership firm before the order had been passed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the impugned order was bad because (a) the District Judge had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order; (b) the procedure prescribed by the Act had not been followed and (c) the order of suspension could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta who had been declared to have been the sole licence in respect thereof. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The power conferred by Section 6 F of the Jammu and Kashmir Act is a legislative one and it cannot be said that the licensing Authority has no jurisdiction under the Rules or to make an order. [578D] (b). The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by section 6 F which implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said Section are present, the licensing authorities had no jurisdiction to suspend the licence. [577E] (c). The procedure prescribed under the statute has been followed in many cases. In some cases, the procedure has been adopted by the authority concerned for issuing a notice or giving an opportunity of hearing and it is not open to the authority to impose any condition which would be contrary to the provisions contained in the statute. [576F] (d) The impugned order passed against the appellants was violative on the principles laid down by this Court in the case of M/s. Todar Mal vs State of Jammu & Kashmir, ; and M/S. Turiam Industries Ltd. vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (e). The order passed under the provisions is not a judicial one but an administrative order which has been passed by an authority subordinate to it. [575F] 2(a). It is not necessary that the grounds on which the order is based should be stated in the order itself or that the reasons for making the order are such as would justify the order being made. The reasons for passing the order have to be communicated to the parties and they cannot be allowed to be prejudiced by the order. The order has to be read in the light of the relevant provisions of law and it must be construed in its entirety. [574C] (g) It is true that the power under Section 6F of the J & K Act is not an absolute one but a legislative power. It can be exercised only by the licensing authori ty, who has to act judicially.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain properties in Pakistan, applied to the Custodian for cancellation of a lease granted by him under section 12 of the , and called upon them to show cause why they should not be evicted. The respondent contended that the notice was ultra vires the powers conferred on him by section 10 of the Act as it applied only to properties of the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself, and that the direction with reference to them were unauthorised. Held, that the power conferred on the Custodian under section 10 is absolute and unqualified and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The right of the appellants to have their rights determined by the notice dated December 2, 1954, was not affected by the amendment. The notice in terms refers firstly to the lease which it is proposed to cancel and secondly to the movables in respect of which certain directions were given. In the present case the notice did not purport to cancel the agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them. The appellants had no authority under section 9 to issue any direction with regard thereto. The power conferred by section 12 was absolute and that it cannot be exercised notwithstanding anything contained therein in any law for ' the timebeing in force. The right to have the rights determined or varied by the rules made thereunder is subject to the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The Custodian had the power under section 11 to cancel a lease, and the notice could not be challenged on the ground that it was ultra rites.

The appellant, a minor son of the respondent Board of Revenue, was assessed to land revenue by the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972. The revision application filed by the respondent was dismissed by the Board of revenue on the ground that the land in possession of Raghubir Singh was ancestral and not ancestral. The appellant preferred a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and remanded the case to the Sub division Officer for fresh determination of the call area afresh. The Board ofRevenue, however, held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant) aged 12 years was a minor daughter of Raghubir singh and used to study in Punjab and further held that the respondent 's land was ancestral. In the ultimate analysis the Member of the Board found that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order of the SubDivisional Officer and, consequently set aside the order dated 5th May, 1976 and remanded it for fresh decision. The matter was taken to the Board by a revision application and the Board directed that the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh may be determined according to the old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to new law i,e. In 1955. The High Court also did not go into the merits of the controversy nor did it decide it in the light of the observations of the board. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 221 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1950 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and there is no section like sub section (2) of Section 224 of the government of India in the Act of 1935 in the State of Rajasthan. [728D] 1.2 The Board has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. In order to be a proper and effective instrument for the purpose of better administration, it is necessary that the Board should have been given an opportunity to show cause why the ceiling limit should not be enhanced or altered. Section 221(1) of the Act provides that the State Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. [700E] 1:3 The Board 's power under section 9 is similar and there are no sections like sub sections (2), (2). [730F] 1 :4 In the instant case, the Board had by its order dated 14th April 1975 directed that "the ceiling area may be fixed according to old law". The High court also did neither go into nor did they decide it. It was for the Sub Divi sion Officer, who committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Boards of Revenue itself.

The appellant, a newspaper employee of the respondent company, was employed in the respondent 's establishment. He was later transferred to the service of the State Government by an order dated June 30, 1982. The services of the employees were terminated on the ground that they had not been paid their wages and other benefits. The appellant challenged the validity of the said orders before the High Court which allowed the writ petition holding that the law reports did not carry any news and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by it on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The High Court also held that the demands made by Deputy Labour Com missioner to comply With the order passed by the Central Government on the recommendation of Justice palekar were unsustainable by the judgment dated August 22, 1983 and hence quashed the demand. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports published by the Ist respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the appellant in their production or publication of the aforesaid law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by Central Government. [787G] 1.2 In view of the fact that the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper, the publication thereof by itself is sufficient to make a law Report a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. [788B] 1:3 The law Reports published by tho Ist respondent contain information about recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [789E] 1 :4 The law report published by a first respondent contained information about the recent events that had taken place at the Supreme court or in any High Courts, which were public bodies, and those are matters In which the Public is interested, the question whether the employees engaged in their Production or publication are entitled to the benefit Of the orders made by Central Govern ment on the recommendations made by Justice P.alekar Award. [781E] 2:5 The law books published by Ist respondent contained news and information about its recent events, comments on them etc. The publication of such items by themselves may not be a public newspaper because according to it the necessary pre requisite of a periodical in order to make them a newspaper was that it should contain mainly publicnews or comments on public news and the books containing authoritative reports for future reference could, by no means, be said to contain news so as to become newspaper. [783F] 2.6 The law records published by 1st respondent are newspaper and the employee employed by Ist Respondent in their produced production or publishing of the same is sufficient compliance with the provisions of the Act. Hence it is difficult to agree with the submission made on behalf of the Ist Respondent that the Law reports do not carry out any news nor that the public was interested in them.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent 's workshop situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay. The agreement was described as an agreement of lease and the licensor had agreed to allow him to occupy and use the premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas the licensor has agreed to permit the licensee to use the said premises under the leave and licence of the licensor for a further period of 5 years. The period of leave and license was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the licensor granted his 'leave and licence ' to the respondent to use and occupy the said Premises for the period of two years and since the licensor did not allow him or any fresh agreement was entered into. The appellant filed an application under section 14(1) (e) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1958 seeking eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had failed to prove that he was a sub tenant of the Respondent. The Small Causes Court held that the appellant had failed in proving that he is a licensee and not a subtenant. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court allowed the revision on the view that the licence was not put an end to by the appellants and that in any event by filing the application for eviction the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the Respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was a tenant and having found that the period was of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. [2181 E] 2.1 In view of the intention of the parties in the document and the facts and circumstances of this case it was a licence and not lease. The respondent could not be said to have granted an express licence to continue or use the demised premises till a suit for eviction is filed against him. [2281 G] 2:2 It is true that the language used in section 14 (1) of Maharashtra Rent control Act, 1961 clearly shows that the legislature intended that the tenant should be deemed to be a licensee if he was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. But the words "in occupation" and "in any event" are not defined in the Act. The word "possession" is used in contradistinction to possession as a right to enjoy property or to use it for a certain period. [2381 E F] 2 :3 In the instant case, the respondent had been described as licensee and was not a tenant. good deal of submission was made before the High court that if it was A lease and not licence, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was no estoppel. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & others vs Shri Vishwa Nath & 5 others, [1987] 2 Scale 27, held that where it cannot be said that there was any error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning, and the High Courts should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. In the aforesaid view of this matter, this appeal must fail as we find no ground to interfere with the decision of the High ' Court.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Dholpur. It merged with the State of Rajasthan on January 26, 1950. The Ruler of the former Jodhpur State became a Part B State of India and became part of the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the new State. On January 26. 1950, the appellant company entered into an agreement with the Ruler of Dhol pur, whereby it was provided that all the rights flowing from laws so continued shall be the assets and liabilities of the Union. The Rulers of Dholnagar, which came into existence on January 1, 1950, were merged in the covenant by a resolution dated December 27, 1950 and the appellant Company was incorporated as a Part C State with effect from January 26th, 1950; but before that date the Ruler had no authority to transfer or assign any part of his rights under the agreement. The appellant company claimed exemption from payment of tax on the ground that it was not liable to pay tax on its sales turnover in respect of the goods sold by it and that the liability of the State was not exempt from taxation. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal holding that the agreement did not bind the appellant as it stood before the merger provision was made for the continuance of laws in the Covenanting State until such time, as they had been modified by a new State; and that even if there was any liability of either the former State of Bikaner or Jaipur to refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was made, that liability did not devolve on the Part B States of Rajasthan under article 295(2) of the Constitution. The High Court also held that the Covenant by which the new state came into force was in its entirety an act of State and that article VI therein could not operate to confer any right on the company as against the new sovereign, for the principle was well settled that clauses in treaties entered into by sovereigns of independent States whereunder sovereignty in territories passed from one to the other providing for the recognition by the old sovereign of the existing rights of the residents of those territories must be regarded as invested with the character of an act or conduct of the new states after it came into operation. Held, that the covenant in question was not a law and the exemption given to the appellant under the Agreement continued. The agreement was not one which created any right in favour of the Ruler but was only a recognition by him of his right to exemption from taxation; it was an act which clearly applied to the Mills and it was held that there was no recognition by, the Union of the right to exempt the appellant from payment tax. The covenant continued till they were repealed or altered recognised that it did not confer any rights on the appellant.

The appellants were the owners of a commercial crop in Madras. They had been selling the same to various persons who had purchased it from the purchasers and had also been paying the price for the commodity purchased at Rs. 1,000 per maund. The appellants contended that they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. Held, that the bye law prohibiting the deduction of trade allowance depends upon the nature of that deduction and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances. The question whether a particular item of expenditure is a trade allowance or not depends upon its nature and character and the object of the statute in making it. If the payment is de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered, it would not be a deduction from the price or commodity within the meaning of section 14 of the Act. The validity of that part of the bye laws prohibiting the deductions of trade allowances depends upon whether the deduction is permitted to be received by the rules or bye laws made under that section. If on the other hand, mahimai ' is a profit allowance, the said part of it would obviously be invalid as inconsistent with the provisions of section 15. The fact that the market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the provi sions but made the byelaw mentioning the ' mahmimai" allowance as one not deductible in any transaction does not lead to the conclusion that the said portion of the Bye law would obviously he invalid as inconsistency with the pro visions of section14.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) There was no inconsistency between the two. There was a clear evidence that all the three lived together and that one was a younger brother and the other a tenant of the appellant in question. The fact that the appellants were also there but had no hand in the killing did not even hit him; and the High Court was right in holding that section 377 of the Code does not abrogate or modify that provision. (ii) There is no reason to depart from this practice in this case and so reduce the sentences of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia to transportation. The sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases also mainly because of the difference of opinion in the High Courts, not only on the question of guilt but also on that of sentence. (iii) There were no reasons to depart with this practice. (iv) There could be no doubt that the conviction was bad as there was no evidence to show that the accused had done anything except be present and even if it be accepted that Nilia aimed a blow, at Ramchander 's thigh he was so half hearted about it that it did not Even hit him. (v) There can be no presumption of common intention in every case of murder under section 377 or section 378 of the Criminal Procedure Code that there is an element of common knowledge between the accused and the deceased. The distinction between a crime committed by a person and another was not a matter of law but one of fact, and it was common ground between them that the act must have been done in furtherance of the common intention of the accused. (vi) There are no compelling reasons to deviate from this rule in this connection.

The petitioner was employed in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) after he had attained the age of 50 years. The petitioner challenged the said order before this Court on the ground that the order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner was promoted as officiating Executive Engineer which is a Class II post on 25.5.1972 and therefore on the date of the order he had completed the age Of 50 years, after he has attained the said age of fifty five years. [637C] 1.2 The object of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Govern ment servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sory retirement is exercised, the Government Servant con cerned must be taken to be in Class I or Class II service or post at the relevant time and would come within the ambit of sub clause (i). [638E F] 1:3 The object and purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j) is that confer power upon the appropriate authori ty to compulsorily retired Government servant In the public interests and the classified categories covered under sub clauses(i) & (ii), has a vestige of discretion. If he is only a temporary hand, he has no right to the post and can always be reverted to the substantive post, if any, on which he has a lien. [625H; 626A] 1 :4 The object underlying Fundamental Rules 55(j) and 56( j) is not to confer powers on the appointing authority to compulsory retire Government servants in the Public interest and to bring about uniformity of treatment in respect of government servants who at the time of their appointment are in Class II or Class 11 service or posts, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. [ 626B] 1;5 The object is to conferring power on appropriate authority in the interest of public service and the differentiation between Government servants who have been appointed de novo may be justified by the purpose of sub clauses.(i) to (ii). If the officer is not in Class 11 or Class I service or Post, he had no right of the post. [ 625C] 2:6 The object for Fundamental Rules56(j), is to conferment power on Government servants to substantive posts in the Govern ment and the distinction between Government servant who are in class I or class II service and those who at that time are in classes I or classes 11 service, whether permanently or temporarily, on officiating or temporary basis. If a Government servant belonging to a Class I and Class II Service or post is in such service orpost as covered by subsection (i), he has an right to tho post and cannot be strictly said to be In that service or the post as a member of that service. [643E F; 626B C] 2.1 Sub clause (ii)(a) of Rule 56 of the Fundamental Rules, which is relevant for the purpose, is to give effect to the policy of the Government in regard to the conditions of service of government serv ers and other employees who are governed by sub cl.(i).

The appellant Corporation issued a notice to the respondent Corporation for payment of the amount of premium payable by it towards the first premium and also for payment thereof. The respondent Corporation did not pay the amount within the stipulated period. The appellant Corporation filed a suit against the respondent corporation for recovery of the sum of money paid by it, on the ground that there was a concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. It was alleged that with full knowledge of the completion of all preliminaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the second premium and therefore it was the case of the plaintiffs respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of the proposal. The Trial Court held that there were no concluded contract of insurance between the appellant Corporation and the respondent. It also noted that it was significant that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposal was as a matter of fact accepted by the Divisional Manager, on behalf of the Corporation, but it was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount was received by the respondent without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of proposal. It further held that the other averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the corporation that the payment of first premium would amount to the acceptance of his proposal were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to acceptance of tho proposal if the proposal Was not otherwise accepted. The High Court also held that having regard to the conduct of the parties, there was no concluded insurance contract between them and therefore the suit was maintainable. Allowing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf the Corporation nor was it proved and secondly because there was nothing to show that such could have been the deposition in law. [359H; 360A] 1.2 In the instant case, the allegation that there is assurance on behalf by the field officers and local agent to the deceased that the payments of first premiums would amount acceptance of a proposal were neither established nor even if it was proved and lastly because there is no evidence that such can have been, the deposition of law. The allegation that the amount paid were appropriated towards the premium and the want of any further action to be done by the deceased did not itself create a contract of Insurance between the respondent and the corporation. [360B] 1:3 In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs in this Court.

The appellant, a company carrying on business in coal and coke oven plants, was granted a certificate of fitness under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of income tax dues from it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that an order granting interim injunction "is final" and as such not appealable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: An order passed by the High 'Court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding is not final within the meaning of article 134(1) (c) since the controversy between the parties when the complaint in respect of offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P.C., could be filed against the appellant, it was held not to be final. [955 B] In the present case, the High court 's order refusing to grant an interim injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. The order refusing the interim injunction does not determine whether the order finally disposes of the rights of the party in dispute or not. [936 C] In view of the decision of this Court in Druva Coal Company vs Benaras Bank, ; , it is clear that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights or liabilities of the ' parties is not a judgment, however cardinal the issue may be. The test of finality according to the court is whether the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, the order will undoubtedly be a final one, but if after the order is made, the suit or proceedings still remain to be tried, and the rights in dispute have to be determined, the ' order is interlocutory. [946 D] In this case, it is not contended that the order of the High .Court amounts to a judgment or decree. The expression "final order" in article 133 (1) means an order which finally determines the points in controversy and brings the case to an end. The question whether an order finally disposing of the right of the plaintiff in dispute is final within article 134 (1)(c) of ' the Constitution has been decided by this Court. In the instant case, therefore, the trial court decided the issue against the respondent and the order was confirmed in appeal by the . High Court.

The petitioners, who were engaged in the manufacture of grey cloth, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of 'the grey cloth in the hands of the processor plus the value as per the provisions of Rule 174 of the Rules. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The assessable value is the value at which the said manufacturer is selling the goods must be the price of the grey cloth or fabric plus the cost of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses. But if the trader who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis would give a declaration to the operator as to what would be his price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessablevalue of the manufactured fabric and excise duty would be charged to the invoice on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at Which he would he selling the grey goods in his market, would include only the price or deemed price at that place. [346G H] 1.2 The value of a job work is not the value for purposes of Rule 173 of the rules. It is necessary to include the processor 's expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to mention the manufacturer 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [347A B] 1:3 The assessable values are the value in which the goods are manufactured by the processor. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value or deemed prices of the raw material in the shape of the finished product or fabric, plus the price cost of such job work performed plus manufac turing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It was necessary to included the processor "s profits" who gets his fabrics processed because those might be postmanufact profits. The value would be Rs.30, being the value on which he is selling these goods in market, and that would include also the cost or deemed value at that places. [348G H; 349A B C] 1 :4 Rule 174 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufacturedby another the information is required relating to the prices at which they said manufacturer was selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price atwhich he is sold must be, the value and the cost for the processing be Rs 5, then in such a case the value would include merely the price, or deemed sale price at the factory gate or deemed to be the assessable valuation of the goods. [349G H, 349A] 1 .5 The value for a job worked is not a value for purpose of Rule 172 of the Cen tral Excise Rules, 1944 but it was necessary in the instant case to include him 's profit.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the respondent Panchayat Samiti in 1963 long before the Amending Act came into force. He was, therefore, entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a Clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961, the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayat. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitled to he considered for appointment but, whether the Panchayat had the right to appoint him to the post of Head Clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June 13, 1973. It could not, therefore have appointed the appellant as a Head Clerk, as it purported merely to do, in January 1974 on an ad hoc basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis. [767B C] 1.2 The fact that the appellant is promoted as a head clerk on an Ad hoc basis in January, 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully to the posts of a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [750E F] 1:3 The right of the appellant to be treated for promotion to the Post of Head Clerks prior to his absorption in Government Service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13 1973 when the Amending Acts came into effect. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right on which the appellant has been appointed as an Adhoc basis or by April 1975, on a permanent basis or on April 1, 1975 on an ex hoc basis, was a term, and condition Of service, What is relevant is not Whether the Panchayat Samitis had the power to appoint the appellant in the post or of a Head clerk prior to its absorption in government service.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math. The suit was decreed by the Civil Judge but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saa and Sarbarakar of the deity. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Amauli properties had been purchased by Mahant Shivshankar Yati, who executed a waqf deed on November 12, 1892 bequeathing various properties to the deity with the intent that arrangements for bhog, deepdan and other expenses be met from them. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclean and must, therefore, be regarded as property belonging to the math or deity. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaiuli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yati. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948, the Amaoli properties were described by Mahant Sheo Shankar Yatti and Sri Thakur as properties of the Math and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. [663 C] 2. The income tax law relating to the assessment proceedings is that of the assessee. The question whether the property can be said to belong to the religious or charitable trust depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [665 D] 3. In regard to those properties, the revenue records mentioned the name of Mahant Sheo Shanker Yati and not that of Math or deity, Sri Thakur, Gokarnendra Mahadeoji. The fact that by virtue of this will the Amalik properties were regarded by Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax is no ground for holding that it was property belonging lo the Math or of the temple. [664 E] 4. In view of the finding that the claim was not accepted by the assessing authority, and that the position in regard to these properties taken in the assessment proceeding was adopted by the Mahant only only for his purpose of escaped personal liability, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They applied for quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. The Custodian General rejected their application on the ground that his jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken away by virtue of the provisions of , (44 of 1954) and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The appellants then applied for restoration of the land to them which was refused by the Deputy Custodian General. The revision application filed by the appellants was rejected by the Custodian General on the view that his power to revise an order had not been taken over by virtue Of section 19 of the Act and the Notification issued thereunder. Held, that the Custodian 's power under the , to allot any property to a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. The power of the Custodian under the . to allot such property to persons or to cancel an allotment existing in favour of a person depends upon the facts of each case and it cannot be said that section 19(1) of the 1954 Act is completely in conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of cancellation of allotment is concerned. The effect of sections 12 and 19 of , is that the displaced person to whom land was allotted "held" the land and was in possession of such property at the date of the notification. The expression "held", therefore, means a managing agent or a managing corporation constituted under that Act. The word "held ' in section 19 (1) does not mean a mere manager or a Managing Agent but includes a managing agency. The words "held". and "held " are used in the context of the definition of "held property" in section 2(d) of . The expression 'held" is not defined in the Act. It is only when the word " held" is used that it would be an evacuee property. The definition of 'held property ' in the , includes a lease or a lease which is granted before the commencement of the , and does not include a lease. The term "held." means a lease, a lease etc., and not a lease for a period of more than one year. The fact that subsequent to the issue of the Notification under section 12(1), the property would cease to be evacuee property, the aforesaid powers of the custodian would be in conflict With those conferred by section 19 Of the 1954 , on a managing officer or a manage corporation constituted by that Act and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women), District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regionalmasters of Girls schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) and Districtaddress of Girls School in Uttar pradesh Educational Service Senior Scale ( Oriya). The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the interview were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission issued a corrigendum on June 8. 1985 to the effect that the result of the written exami nation shall be reviewed and re opened. The State Public Service commission had undertaken a recruitment to fill up the vacancies in accordance with the rules. The appellants who were unsuccessful candidates filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written re spondents in regard t he written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the viva voce test from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina t tion. On behalf of respondent State it was submitted that when there was a mistake pointed out, there had been no justification to cancel the written parts of the ap peals and drive the candidates to litigation. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has upheld the actions of the public Service Commission and has dismissed the Writ Petitions. [ 126F] 1.2 In the instant case, when no defects were pointed out by the Public Serv ices Commission in regard thereto, there Was no justification warranting cancellation of the entire recruitment examination and drive ting the candidates for litigation. The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not had suffered. Public time would not has been wasted in requiring re doing of what had once been done and the litigation could have be avoided. [127F G] 1:3 The situation was could have had been appropriately meet by setting it aside, setting aside tho recruitment and asked for a 126 fresh interview on the conclu sion of the two examinations and select those who on the base of the result thereof success would not get disturbed. There was no reason to cancel that part of recruitment examinat ion and drive a candidates to litigations. On the facts alleged, it is directed that the results of the re opened shall be finalised within four months hence.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. The defendant contended that the Dhoti was an independent Dera, that he was in possession of properties of the dera as its lawful mahant; that the appellant had no right to recover possession of that property of the deceased Dera; that he had no locus standi to file the suit and that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy was raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the dead person within the time prescribed by law. The High Court also held that after S 's death, Shia Ram as his chela "Inherited, the sum of total of rights which already vested in the Dio could make no difference when he was elected as mahant of the S ' and that there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as a mahant to succeed him. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The suit was filed on the basis that the plaintiff as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of Dera at Landeke, that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant and entitled to management the properties; and that he could be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [490C] 2. The subject matter of the suit is the interest of Som Das in the S Dera. Som Dass. He was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahants of the Rera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as ma Mahant subsequent to the death, of Som Chand. [491D] 3. The question whether the interest in the subject matter was the interest or the property of a party in the C 's representative capacity or not depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. [492E] 4. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest, of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22 Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [483G] 5. The rule that had to be apply is Order 21, rule 1, r. 10, and not Rule 3 or 5, whether devolution takesplace as a result of death, or for some other reason.[494C D] 6. When the suit has been brought by a party or against any person in representative capacity, there is no devolution of interest during the pendency of a suit and the elected persons can be added to as parties in order 22, Rule 10 notwithstanding the fact that the periods of limitation prescribed for impleading themselves under Order 21 rule 1 have expired. In Roshan Lal vs Kapur Chand the Court took the view that newly appointed trustees are not legal representatives or of the trustees who had filed the suit, and thereafter died during the course of the litigation, that they can be add as parties to under Order 2, Rule 3 notwithstanding the period that the limitation for impleaded them had elapsed. [504E] 7. The Court said that where some of the members die or retire during the proceedings of a case and new persons are elected to fill their place, it is a case of devolution of interests during the pending suit but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the court.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were Government employees of the State Government. They challenged the Ordinance on the ground that it was unreasonable and arbitrary, that the reduction of the age of retirement from 58 to 55 was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution; that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that as a result of the increase in the age Of retirement from 55 to 58, the Government of Andhra Pradesh by a notification dated October 29, 1979 reduced the age to 5 i; that providing employment opportunities to the youths h Is no relevance on the question of fixing the age for retirement, and that the decision of the Government was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the questions of the fixation of the retirement; and that it had acted arbitrarily in not granting any previous opportunity to the petitioners which would enable them to provide their affairs. The State Government contended that the question as regards the age was a pure question of Governmental policy affording no cause of action to the Petitioners to file the writ petitions, and the decision which the Government took later to increase the age from 55to 58 years was not based on the recommendation of the Commission. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The reduction of retirement of experienced and mature persons from Government service will result in grave detriment to public services of the state; and, therefore, the decision is bad for non application Of mind to relevant facts bearing on this question of the date of retirement. [939E] 2.1 The Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixationof the age. It was later in October 1979 that the State Govern ment had recommended increase the retirement of their employees to 55, though it was earlier increased from 55 and not 58; that by a Notification dated September 17, 19,9 the recommendations of the Third Central Pay Commission were accepted by the Government but, not so the recommendation regarding increasing the age is not accepted by Government initially because, it felt that raising the age would reduce employment opportunities in the immediate future. By a notification issued on September 17 19, 979 the recommendations regarding increased age of superannuation from 55 are accepted by State Government and consequently, the ageof retirement was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l9 1979. [936C D] 2:2 The question as regard the age or retirement is a pure questions of Governmental Policy affording no causes of action, to the petitioner to file writ petitions. It is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. No. The contention of the petitioners that the amendment of February 17, 1983 to Fundamental Rules was made by the State in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitu tion cannot be accepted because of our conclusion that the enhancement of the superannuation from 58 is not hit by Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not discriminatory or unreasonable. [946E F] 2 :3 The Government was estopped from reducing the age and retirement from 60 to 58 years, since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the retirement from55 to 58. It would have been a different matter if the Government felt that raise the age at 55 years instead of 55 to 60, it might have decided to reduce the age but it was later by way of amendment of the Fundamental Rules. The Government could not have altered the conditions of service of employees who had acted in excess of their powers under the proviso.

The appellants are dealers in milk and milk products. They purchase raw materials from outside the State of Haryana. The assessees claimed exemption under section 24(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 on the ground that they were not liable to pay tax on the sales made by them in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim and held that the purchases were not exempt from tax u/s 9(1)(b) of that Act. On appeal, the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute; and (ii) the effect of the decision is that the words 'disposes ' used in cl. (a) (ii), later, cl.(b) above was compre hensive enough to include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than by way of sale in the State or despatches the manufactured product to a place outside the state in any manner otherwise than through way of sales in the con tract in the nature of local sale; and that the effect is that, the words `disposes" used therein should be construed as including cases of despatch of goods from one place to another. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words 'or despatches ' are not defined in the Act. They are wide enough to take within their sweep all sales made in the process of export out of the territory of India. [351B] 1.2 In the instant case, the purchases of raw materials by the assessees were not charge able to tax either u/S 9(i) or section 6 or section 24 (3). The purchases of such raw materials were not con tractable to tax under section 9(3) and therefore, they were exempt from payment of tax. [352C] 1:3 The words "or despatching the manufactured products to a factory outside the territory in any way otherwise than for by way sale in tho State" are wide and include all sales effected in the ordinary course of export outside the country. [353E] 1 :4 The effect of decision is, that the goods presently in question are not laible to tax u /s 9 (1) or s 6 or s 24(3). [352F] 2.1 In cases covered by section 5(3), the words, 'disves sion of ' and despatches them to a places outside the States in any ways otherwise than on way of inter state trade or com pensation ' in the evi dence of export within the meaning of sub section (1). [353G] 2:2 The effect is, therefore, that words "and despatches" are not included in cl.(a)(i) later clause (ii). [355H] 2 :3 In cases where the manufactured articles are disposed of only by way 'penultimate sales falling under section 5 (3), but not under section 6 and s 24 (1), but, not under Section 5(1), the goods still in question were not laable to Tax either u /S 9 (i). [356B] 2.(a) The effect would be that the word 'dis condi tions ' is used in the sense of 'sale ' and not in the context of sale. [355C] 2(b)(ii). In cases falling under Section 6, the goods then in question being not la posed to tax, they are not taxable either u s 9 (I) or Section 6 or Section 24(2).

The appellants were the owners of certain goods which had been exported by them to their buyers. The sales tax authorities held that the sellers were not entitled to the benefit of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution and that the sales were exempted from tax under article 286 (1)(a). Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) mean " a registered dealer to whom he has sold the goods. The words " such person " are used in the sense in which they are understood in the ordinary parlance of the word. The intention of the parties that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of Imports & Exports Control Act 1947, the property is intended to pass and does pass on the shipment of the goods must be held to have taken place "in the course of export" and the exemption under article 285(1) (b) will come into operation. The object of the law was not to levy purchase tax on a person who has given such certificate under section 8(b). The words used in cl. (a) are " a dealer to which he has sells the goods ". It is only when the goods were not 'despatched outside the State of Bombay that the purchasing dealer may not be liable for having made a false declaration". The intention was not merely to avoid payment of tax but also to prevent evasion of tax. The word " a " person" in section 8 must mean a registered or a registered "dealer to whom the goods are sold. It is not necessary that the person should have been a registered ' dealer as sufficient. The fact that the goods had been despatched by him or by a person to whom they were sold would not make any difference. The mere fact that he was not a registered and registered dealer did not make it clear that the intention of Parliament was to levy tax on him. The expression " a" in cl.(a) means " a 'registered dealer to whose goods are sent. " It is true that the word " person " has been used in section 5(b), but the use of the words ' a registered" in the context of the export would not justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales had been onmine contracts property in the goods would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. The time of the sale should be interpreted as the time when the customs frontier is crossed and that it was the intention Of the Legislature to levy Purchase Tax on a "person who has give such certificate ".

The appellant, a married woman, was married to the respondent on May 15, 1962. The appellant filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 before the Magistrate who tried the petition for the maintenance of herself and her child. The Magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 127(3) (b) had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court allowed the revision petition and held that there was no settlement by consent decree in 1962 whereby the appellant 's client was still entitled to an allowance. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 A divorcee is not entitled to claim under section 126(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. The provision in the Explanation (b), however, does not apply to cases where the husband has been divorced by his wife and the consent decree. [81 E] 1.2 In the instant case, there was a settlement by mutual consent between the parties whereby the mehar money had been paid and all claims adjusted, and so no claim for maintenance could survive. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available but there is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962 they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. No settlement of claims which does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 124 can operate to nullify that claim. Payment of meharmoney, as a customary discharge, is within the cognisance of that provision. [82 E F] 1:3 The consent order of 1962 decided all disputes between the appellant and her husband. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. The purpose of payment 'under any customary or Personal law ' must be to obviate destitution of the wife and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [83 E F; 83 A] 1 :4 The whole scheme of section 127 (3) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the party. There should be a reasonable relation between tho sum so received and its actual potential as provided for maintenance, and the provision for Maintenance. [84 E F]. The object of the payment ' under any customary law or personal Law ' must he to obviate the destitutionof the divorceee and to providing her with whereverwithal, to maintain himself. The whole Scheme of section 125 (4) (a) is clearly to recognise that the substitute Maintenance arrangement by lumpsum payment organised through the custom by the community has a reasonable relationship to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 488 not mathematically but fairly then section 127.(3) subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The object is manifestlyto recognise the substituted maintenance arrangement from by lump payment organised at by the Custom of the Community or the Personal law of parties.

The appellant was the highest bidder for a sum of Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction of his shop held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor shop but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Nath Village Repura, P.S. Pusa, Distt. Samastipur was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector, Samastiharpur. The appellant was given the premises of shop No.3, Pusa District Samastidastipur and he did deposit the amount as required by Rule 3(1) of the Bihar Excise Rules, 1915. The respondent was asked to deposit the same in the office of the Collector on 25th March, 1988. The Collector did not accept the proposal of black listing the appellant but deposited the amount in the Office of the Collectorate. The letter dated 25th April, 1988, stated as follows: "The Collector after perusal of the said office note passed order on 25.3 .88 which is produced in verbatim below: Ist bidder chunki defaulter hai atah security prapt kar raita ke liae Black list karen. " The appellant deposited the money in the Collectorate on 25/3.1988 and he was asked by the respondent to deposit Rs. 11,900 for the purpose of depositing the amount. On 25th May 1988, the Collector passed an order directing that the appellant be placed in black list under the order passed by Collector. The order stated as "The collector after perusal and hearing the appellant, cancelled the bid of the appellant and directed that the name of the respondent be placed In the black List for future. This order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collec tor. The appeal filed against this order was dismissed by the Commissioner. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 Rule 3 of the Excise Rules is not mandatory and it has to be realised that black listing any person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. [868H; 869A] 1.2 Rule 3 does not require specifically of giving any notice before black listing anyone. The rule of law that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural Justice is not a universal principle of law. It has to he realised that Black listing any persons in respect Of business v Issues has civil consequences for the past business of a person concerned In any event, even if the Rules do not expressly express so it is not an elementary rule of natural law that parties effected by any orders should have rights of being represented and making representation against the said order. The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appel lant in respect o future contracts, cannot be sustained in law.

The property, which was the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1, originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and measuring 41 grounds and 2005 sq. 534/66, the Court, on a perusal of the sale deed dated 30.7.53 filed by the LIC before it came to the conclusion that the buildings on the land leased under exhibitP 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect of this premises also. The Rent Controller fixed the fair rent at Rs.994 p.m. and directed the LIC to pay the same to the appellant within a period of two months from the date of receipt of the order. The LIC filed an appeal before the High Court against the said order. In the meantime, the LIC filed a suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Controller 's order in respect thereof. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court and the High court confirmed the decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether an order in the earlier proceedings is to be treated as an order passed totally without jurisdiction although it has become final as be tween the parties? When a petition under section 4 is filed, the Rent Control ler, on the language of section 4 has to decide: (i) whether the applicant is a tenant in, or landlord of, the building and (ii) what the fair price of the premises should be in accordance with the provisions of the Act. It will not be open to the civil court to re determine the rent payable by the tenant to the landlord because that is a matter squarely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Rent controller. [549C D] 1.2 The question on which the jurisdiction is excluded is only the determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. If the civil Court in this case had come to the conclu sion that there was a relationship of landlord and tenant and that tho LIC was not entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the LIC on the basis of the fair value fixed by the Rent Authori ties. [550E F] 1:3 The question as to whether the order in this earlier proceedings was to be regarded as an Order passed totally Without jurisdiction, although it had become final, as it has been rendered final as a result of the decision on his part that either the applicant was not a ryot or the land is not ryoti land; in the instant case, it was the latter and such decision on the nature or character of the land has been given a finality under section 64 C which cannot be ques tioned in a court of law. [551C D E] 1 :4 The question of ouster of the civil suit 's jurisdiction as well as the provisions o the Act, does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [552F] 1 5.1 In an application under section4, the jurisdiction to decide whether the application in the later proceedings is a ryoti or not is to determine a fair or neces sary rent for tho premises. The answer, in our opinion, has to be in the negative. There is no doubt that, since an application for this purpose cannot lie except at the instance of a landlord or tenant, the rent Controller has to deal with this incidentally but this is not one of the direct issues before the Rent inves tigation. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, theRent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what thefair rent is and then fades out of the picture.

The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the High Court. The petition er challenged the final inter State seniority list on the ground that he was not heard after the final list was prepared. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the case now before it is governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case with reference to an entirely different and provisional list of Forest Officers. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner respondent was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the final seniority list was to be declared and published as a final list. [838E] 1.2 In order to establish the invalidity of the final gradation list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. The decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration ation, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [828G] 1:3 In order that a particular judge may go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government, it would necessarily be fair to give a person affected an 'oppo rtunity to be heard against the proposed list before it was finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts, may be rectified. [829B C] 1 :4 The petitioner re spondent was claiming relief against the final Inter State seniority List although he was given due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. He is a respondent before us. [827E F] Shankariah vs Union of India, ; , followed.

Raj nikant Brothers case ( supra). The petitioners have been denied the facility which has been given by the respondents under the Export Policy for 1978 79 on the basis of exports made in 1977 78.
