A close examination of the Import Trade Policy 1978 80 under which the petitioners have obtained the Additional licences and the import and Export Houses, shows that there is material difference between the conditions for grant of Additional Licences granted under Import Policy1978 79 and the conditions of eligibility for grant thereof under the Imprestary Licence issued to export House Certificate as well as grant of additional licences to export houses under the Foreign Trade Policy 198891. The appellant company was manufacturing and selling the goods in packed condition. The packing material was to be supplied by the buyer to the assessee at the factory gate. The containers were not returnable by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value. The appellant contended that on a correct interpretation of section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the cost of packing could be included In the assessable Value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the asses see to the buyer, in respect of all other costs of packing, the costs should be included. The Revenue contended that the value of packing materials including those supplied by it had to he included in its assessable value only when they were sold at the time of removal in packed conditions and the containers were therefore not returnable to by the purchaser, there was no reason for the appellant to include the cost incurred by the manufacturer when the pack is supplied by him. The Tribunal held that the cost price of packing envisaged in section 4 (4)(D)(i), did not in clude within its ambit the cost for packing not incurred by it when the containers are supplied by a buyer and not the manufacturer, and therefore, the sale value had also to be excluded from the assessable valuation. The revenue appealed to this Court against the Tribunal 's order. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 In cases where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of the excisable goods, while determining the value, of such goods, the Cost of packing where the excisable article is delivered at the place of removal, in packed Condition, would have to be added to the price except where the packing was of durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. The "cost of such pack ing" referred in section4(4) (d)(ii) does not in elude within their ambit the costs of pack ing not incurred wholly by the manufacturers when the packed is supplied at the depot gate. [982A] 1.2 In cases, where the statute provides for duty with respect to value, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. In this view of the matter, it is unnecessary to discuss wider questions as to the circumstances in which the cost o packing (primary or secondary) can at all enter into the determination of the assessablevalue under section 4.(4)(c)(i). [987C D] Union of India & Ors. vs Godfrey Phillips, by the learned Attorney General. [1989] Suppl. 1 S.C.R. 981; Union of lndia vs Godafrey Philips, ; , referred to. 1.3 The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression "assessable value" as interpreted in section before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the amend ment intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost" rather than "value", the nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that, while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at a factory gate is to be taken as the assessable values, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the sale price, the manufacturers levies a charged for the pack ing which is 475ically and necessarily incidental to placed placing the finished product on the Market. [990D E] Union Of India & Anr. vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd., ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and under section 336 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 1 informed him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of Rs. 50/ . The appellant was stated to have pressed the demand to PW 1. PW 2, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, on the same day. PW 6 after drawing up a mahazar in the presence of PW 2 and PW 7, handed over the money to the appellant who received the same. The appellant produced the currency notes. The test was positive, the currency note were seized and the appellant arrested. The trial court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appellant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the accused had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant. was guilty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction under section 165 I. P.C., and section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act are to be maintained. [337E] 2.1 In a case where the accused person has received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration, the court is required to draw a presumption that the person receiving it as a motive of reward such as is mentioned in section 161, I.p.C.; and this burden rests on the accused persons in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation tendered by the accused is reasonable and probable. [340E F] 3.1 The onus resting on the prose cution person in such cases would not he as light, as it was where a statutory presumption is raise under section 113 of Evidence Ac tion Act and not on proof of the same facts. [341G H; 342A] 4.2 In the instant case, the appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. The case that has been developed in the course of the trial is not that of a loan transaction but payment of an advance of Rs . 50/ by PW 1 has not been even suggested. It cannot therefore be said that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant, [342B] 5.3 In the present case, it could not be said to have been consistent con strued with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW I. The prosecution evidence that has developed in course of trial is also not impressive. It can therefore be held that the appe lant had even on preponderance of probabilities succeeded in proving his guilt. [342C] 6.4 In the case of Dipawali gift or return, of a loans given to PW1 has not not been specifically suggested. The evidence that had been developed by the pro duced appellant is clearly incon sistent with the transactions of loan and return of a ted loan or ' return of loan advanced to PW I has not be en quired. [343D] 7. In the absence of any cogent explanation for his failure to examine PW 1 and till 22.10, 1975, the file itself was kept by the appeli lant in his personal custody.

The petitioner was an officer or employee of a company. He was prosecuted for wrongful withholding of property belonging to the company and for wrongful recovery of such property by issue of process under section 630(1) of the . The prosecution alleged that the petitioner had wrongfully taken possession of certain properties belonging to him, wrongfully withholds it or knowingly applies it to purposes other than those expressed or directed in the articles and authorised by the Act. The trial court acquitted the petitioner but on appeal the High Court held that the term 'officer or employee ' used in sub section (1) was referable to existing officers and employees of a Company and not to former officers and employee, and that the phrase 'any such property ' in cl. (a) qualify the words 'any property of a " company" appearing in cl.(b) and (b) of sub section(1). Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'any person ' occurring in sub s.(1) is not confined only to existing employees or employees but also to past officers and servants if such officer or employees either (a), wrongfully obtains possession of any property of the company during the course of his employment. [176G] 2. The words 'such property ' used therein are wide enough to include past officers, and employees, and even to past employees or employee, would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl.(b) as applicable to such property of another company, possession of which is wrongfully obtained by an officer/employee of the Company i.e. refers to the whole of cl. [177A B] 3. The word 'officer ' in sub sec.(1), means a person who has been placed in possession of property of any company as mentioned in cl(a) and includes past officers or employees if such officers or employee either (i) wrongfully obtains Possession of any such property during the pendency of his appointment, to which he is not entitled. [179C] 4. The term 'Officer ' used by section 630 of the H 172 Act is wide enough not only to include all existing officers but also includes past employees and employees if the officer or employer either (b), wrongfully withholdes possession of such properties after the termination of his services. [180D E] 5. The Legislature has deliberately enacted sub s(1), which is a penal provision, for the recovery of property by the issue of processes under section 634(l)(b) against such officer and employee. It is not correct to say that the legislature intended that the word 'Officer or employee" should be interpreted in its widest sense so as to include only past officers but not to past officials and employees. [181E] 6. The whole object of enacting sub section 1 of section 630 is the preservation of the property of an "company by the creation of two distinct offences by clauses (a)(b), (c) and(d). It would be rendering nugatory by throwing cl. in the form of a penal clause which provides that all such officers and other employees shall, on the complaint of the companies or creditor or contributory thereof, be punishable with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees. [182F H] 7. The language of sub s. (1), namely, 'if any officer or servant of a ' company wrongfully withhold ' possession of ' such property after the terminated of his service. ' is not restricted only to past Officers and employees but includes past officials or employees, if such Officer or employee neither (a). wrongfully obtains actual possession of the said property during that period nor does he obtain possession of it after the expiry of the period of employment.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. He installed in the temple a permanent structure on it all along its property and dedicated to the deity. The deity installed in his temple a temporary shed on it. The temple was managed by the appellant as manager of the temple. The appellant 's claim for the temple was rejected by the Charity Commissioner. In appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the Charity Com missioner. In this Court, HELD: (1) There is absolutely no evidence in this case about dedication to the public or public user of the Temple as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities to foster maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole. [530 D] (2) The Sansthan and the temple are public religious endowments. That would, however, not lead to the conclusion that the property is a private or a public religious endowment. [ 527 E F] (3) There was absolutely no reliable evidence in support of the contention that the Sansthan and its endowment were public religious trusts. [525 G] (4) The appellant had been running a temporary temple for more than a century as a result of which he installed in another temple a regular shed on the land all along his property and the site thereof. It is clear from the recitals of the deed that the dedication was made with the object of maintenance of worship of deity for its benefit. [455 G] The Sansthan was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindus, as a part of the family. It had been managed by a saints in succession as Manager not as personal or private property. [ 526 B C] (5) There were no evidence to show dedication to any public or private institution. The mere fact that the temple is a public trust does not make it a public endowment. When the origin of an endowment is obscure and no direct oral evidence is available, the Court will have to resolve the controversy about the character of the trust on documentary evidence, if any, the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in Which the property had long been used by the public, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes as a matters of right Without the least interfere or restriction From the above, the appellant contends that the Sanad being an ancient Royal grant is a very important piece of evidence to prove that although Sakharam Maharaj, the founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the saintts in descended by the reigning saint.

The petitioner was arrested and detained in jail in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for the recovery of the demand certified under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act. The petitioner contended that (i) section 46 (2) Of the Indian Incometax Act offended article 14 of the Constitution and (ii) that section 13 Of the Bombay Provincial Land Revenue Code, 1879 was violative of article 22(1) and (2), article 14 and article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of all the State laws are mutatis mutandis to be read into section 46 of the Act and that therefore if there be any vice of discrimination in the State law that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section46(2). The grouping of the income tax defaulters into separate categories or classes Statewise is certainly a territorial classification which is based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purposes of the recovery Of their own public demands, cannot be regarded by itself as bereft of a reasonable nexus or correlation between the basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Indian income tax Act any more than it can be so regarded with respect to the respective State laws. The group making of the Income tax defaulters in separate categories and classes State wise is certainly one territorial classification, which is founded on an differentia and that the sub rejection, for, the purposes Of recovery of their own Public demands, could not be regarded 'as bereft of any reasonable nexus nor correlation between tho basis of discrimination and the objects sought to he achieved by it. The Indian Income Tax Act by section 46 has been amended and the warrant of detention was issued on the 7th June 1955, that is to say, long after the amendment of the section. The nature of the tax is one and the same, and it is levied under a single Central Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and extent between State and State.

The appellants were the trustees of a Port Trust Employees ' Union. The Trustees, therefore resolved that the shore crew at the Alexandra Docks should work for 8 hours and that there should be a variable recess of one hour and overtime of three hours should be paid. On the other hand, the Act and the Rules fix the number of hours of work, payment of overtime and for hours of rest in the work day of the workman. The appellants contended that section 13 fixes the number Of hours of duty, payment Of overtime and overtime for hours and hours of part in the working day and that the number is inclusive of one or more specified intervals. Held, that the total number of days of work in a week is 48 hours per day for 6 days overtime and not the number as fixed by the Act or the Rules. The period of work of an adult worker in a factory shall be so arranged that inclusive of his intervals for rest under section 55 they shall not spread over more than ten and a half hours in any day; provided that the Chief Inspector may increase the spread over to 12 hours on any day and work up to 9 hours on such day. The words "inclusive of one" or "two" are used in the context of the scheme of compels the inclusion of an hour of rest into a normal working day. Rule 25(1) which says that the maximum number of workers of an establishment shall be 48 hours, though on any particular day the hours of the work in the week do not exceed 48, although on any specific day the time of work is not specified. The total number Of days of overtime worked in a year is 48 (8 hours per week for 6) days overtime.

The appellant was the owner of a house let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and thereafter the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection under this Act. The landlord filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment of the appellant on the ground that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 years in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972, provisions of this Act will be applicable to the present case and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the revision petition set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as during the pendency of this matter in this Court 10 years have not been completed and therefore the High court passed the decree Now it could not be contended that as till the matter was pending in the High Courts, 10 years had elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1. In view of this the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Section 20 of the Act because according to him the appeal will be a continuation of the suit and therefore he advantage will be available. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right of the parties will be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date when the suit was filed. But in Vineet Kumar 's case (supra) this Court took the view that if during the course of proceedings 10 years has elapsed the tenant is entitled to benefit of Section 2 restriction of the institution of suit as provided for in Section 20 clause (1) quoted above will not be applicable and it is thus clear that during the period 1.10.86, 10 year have to be computed from 1.12.87 but this contention could not been accepted as it was very clear from the language used in the said provision that it applied only to a suit pending on the day of commencement of the . [167F H] 1.2 The appellant tenant cannot claim protection under Section 20 because of the wording of Section 39 and section 40 even if he is entitled for the benefit under this section even if his case is pending in this court. [167C D] 1:3 In the instant case, the suit giving rise to the instant appeal was filed on 23rd March, 1974 long after the commencement of this Court and therefore restriction as provided in Section 2 restrictions of the Institution of suit is not attracted and it was thus clear from a reading of Section 40 that it applies only to suits pending on that date. [168E F] 1 :4 The contention advanced by the appellant that because of language of Section39 and 40 even assuming that the matter is pending before this Court in this case, and 10 years having elapsed, the appellant will be entitle to the advantage of the Section even if it is held that the rights of parties have to he determined in respect of the date on which the suit is filed still because of this language of section 39 and the appellant is entitled only to the benefits of the provision of this Section. [169F G] 1 .5 The contention of the learned counsel could not therefore be accepted as the matter has been pending in that Court and 10 year has elapsed, i.e., 10 years. It is no doubt true that the appeal is the continuation of a suit and if within the language Of Section 39 the appellant 's right will be governed by the provisions even if this point is pending. [170G H] Om Prakash Gupta vs Smt.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 as amended by the West Bengal Thika Amendment Act, 1952. The trial court held that the tenancy of the respondent was governed by the Thika Tenant 's Protection Act, 1950 and the definition of a thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On appeal the High Court held that at the time when the appeal of the defendant was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by Thika Tenants ' Protection Act of 1950 and that the definition was not retrospective only because the landlord had not filed a plaint in accordance with section 3 of the Act but also under section 4 of the Ordinance. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant tenant that (i) the provisions of the Thiyka Tenancy Acts were prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord could not be said to have failed to establish his existence; (ii) the tenancy in question was governed under the Thirika Tenants Protection act of 1950 which came into force on 21st October before the commencement of the West Benares Thika Thika ' Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952 and therefore section 4 Of the Act would be applicable. HELD: (i)(a) The provisions of section 4 and 5 being prospective and not as such applied to pre existing suits, they were inapplicable to the pre existing suit. [519 C] (b) Section 4 of Act was prospective only and it could not apply to this case. [525 E] (c) The correct view is that sections 4 and 6 being prospective, the landlords had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed. [511 F] (d) The right of the landlord to eject a thikka tenant after the Act had come into force could not therefore be said that he was entitled to protection under the Act as amended.

The appellants were appointed as Section Officers in the secretariat of the State of U.P. on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were promoted to the post of Section Officer by an order dated July 2, 1976. The appellants challenged the said order before the High Court which allowed the writ petition and directed the State Government to give them pay scale equal to Section Officers or Private Secretaries. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order, the appellants filed a Writ Petition in the High court which was dismissed. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the principle of "equal pay for equal work" has no application to the case of the petitioners; (ii) the Court had not agreed with the classification made under the Rules, and (iii) the High Courts were in error in holding that the State Govern ment had granted uniform pay scale of Rs. 1600 2950 to both the grades of Bench Secretaries. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of 'equal pay ' for equal Work has to be construed in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge ing with the adminis tration in fixing pay scales has to he left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [306G H] 2. The High Court had completely overlooked the criterion provided under the rules, the merit governs the grant of higher pay scales and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. The classification made tinder the Rules cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay for Equal work. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our attention that the Court Secretaries Grade I are selected by a Selection Committee. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay Scale. [307D E] 3. The State Government has granted uniform Pay scale of pay of Rs 1600 2900 to both these grades of Judges with effect from January 1, 1986. It is against this background that the principle has to been construed in first place.[308G H; 308A] 4. One can deny that sometimes the difference was a matter which of degree or that there was an elementof value judgmentby those who were charged with administration in fixation of pay scales have to be left with him and it could not be interfered by the court unless it was demonstrated that neither it is wholly irrational nor based on any basis or arrive mala fide, either in fact or in law. [308C] 5. The Court Secretaries, therefore cannot claim as of right the pay scale admissible to Section officers. The question is whether there can be two scales of Pay in the same cadre of persons performing the same or similar work or duties. The Bench Secretaries Grade 1 are selectedby a Selection Commis sioner. The Rules thus make it a proper selection for the purposes of entitlement for higher pay ment scale. [309D E; 308F] 6. The pay scale recommended by the Pay Commission is as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 50 two posts of Bench Secretary Grade II and the posts of Benches Secretaries Grade III and the post in the scale of ` Rs.500 1,000. The respondent, a sugar undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling coal. The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. It had its registered office at Korba, Madhya Pradesh. Its factory was situated within the limits of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi. The respondent was a sugar mill. The sugar mill was used for manufacturing coal from the sugarcane fields. The company was also carrying on business in the said sugar mill and it was supplying coal to various industries. The Company was also maintaining its own machinery, plant and machinery. The Respondent was assessed to property tax under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961. The State Government issued a notification dated March 31, 1976 levying property tax on the respondent 's factory. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had waived its power of taxation by that agreement and, therefore, the imposition of property tax was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that since sugar is a declared industry under the Industrial (Development & Regulation)Act, 1951, Parliament alone was competent to pass a law on the subject and the State Legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by the State legislature on Special Area Development Authorities to impose property tax upon lands and buildings is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred under the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government to regulate and develop the Coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. [23D] 2. The Constitution of India has been enacted by Parliament to provide for the development and administration of Special Areas through special Area Development authorities, Section 64 of the Act of 1973, which provides for the constitution of the special areas, lays down by sub section (4) that: "Notwithstanding anything contained in the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 or the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Panchayats Act, 1962, the Municipal Council, Notified Area Committee or a Panchayat, as the case may be, shall, in relation to the Special area and as from the date the Special Area development Authority undertakes the functions under clause (v) or clause (vi) of section 68 cease to exercise the powers and perform the function and duties which the Special Areas Development Authority is competent to exercise and perform under the Act. " The power of the State Legislatures on Special Areas is eroded only to the extent to which control was assumed by the Union Govern ment pursuant to the declaration made by Parliament in respect of a declared Industry and that the field occupied by such enactment was the measure of the erosion of the legislative competence of the state legislature. [24E F] 3. It was held by this Court that the State Government had waived their power of tax by that Agreement and, consequently, the levy of property Tax was invalid.[25F G] 4. The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 127A of the Municipalities Act and section 135 of the Corporation Act. [26G] 5. Section 127A(2) of Madhya pradesh Municipal Corporation and section 136 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act also provide that the property tax shall not be leviable, inter alia, on "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union government".

The appellant was the lessee of a mining lease granted to him by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was in for a term exceeding one years it was enforceable against him. The appellant filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the ground that the Government had no power under section 20 (1) to terminate the lease. The High Court held that the words " such rights" in the third proviso to sub section (2) of section 20 were not intended to refer to the rights created after July 1 1945, mentioned in the previous proviso and on that construction the lease in favour of the appellant could be terminated only in accordance with that proviso by giving three months ' notice. The question for determination was whether the termination of the lease by the Board of revenue was valid or not. Held, that the word "such rights" used in the second sub section must mean those created before the notified date but after July1, 1945 for a periods exceeding one month would be valid and enforceable both by and against the State Government. The words "such right" in section 20 of the Act are wide enough to include all rights created before that date but they cannot be limited only to those created after the 1st July, 1945.
